title: Trade Secret Societies

detail.title: Trade Secret Societies

publicationDetails.detailsText: NYU Law and Economics Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: NYU Law & Economics Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: NYU School of Law, Public Law Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: NYU School of Law, Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Trade secret law is premised on secrecy, though it has not yet contended with the individual and social effects of keeping and leaking secrets in the psychological and sociological literature on secrecy. This Article introduces that literature and uses it to make the case that secrets make secretholders feel like part of an exclusive club or secret society, fostering loyalty and bonds to their employer in a way that can explain trade secret law's encouragement of corporate secrets. At the same time, this body of literature explains why and when secretholders might be tempted to disclose the secrets they know, also clarifying trade secret law's prohibition of many such disclosures as misappropriation. Moreover, because some secretkeeping can be personally or socially harmful, this literature also provides a framework to analyze when it might make sense for trade secret law to permit-or even encourage-the disclosure of corporate secrets. This overarching understanding also unifies the predominant, but separate, theories of trade secret law-as an incentive to innovate (or reduce secretkeeping costs) and as a regulation of commercial morality. It also provides a basis for a burgeoning view of trade secrecy law as protective of employees, not just businesses. In addition to providing a new conception of trade secrecy, this literature sheds light on how trade secret law might be modified to better accord with society's use for and of secrets.

title: Green Illusions? The Economics of Electric Vehicles in China
affiliations: , National University of Singapore, The Chinese University of Hong Kong - CUHK Business School and National University of Singapore (NUS), Department of Economics

detail.title: Green Illusions? The Economics of Electric Vehicles in China
detail.abstract: This study evaluates whether electric vehicles (EVs) in China have delivered on their “green” promise by improving air quality and reducing private ownership costs. Combining city–month data on EV adoption and air pollution with detailed vehicle-level transaction records, we find little evidence that rising EV adoption reduces concentrations of major pollutants or greenhouse gases. Both the traditional instrumental variable (IV) and the Bartik IV estimations show that the null effects persist after addressing potential endogeneity. The limited environmental gains are largely attributable to the continued dominance of coal in electricity generation and to a sizable rebound effect whereby lower operating costs increase vehicle usage. On the private side, although EVs reduce energy expenditures by roughly CNY 16,747, their faster depreciation leads to an average net loss of about CNY 18,175 over the ownership period relative to fuel vehicles (FVs). Counterfactual simulations show that EVs match the emissions of fuel vehicles when the coal share falls to about 55%, deliver measurable benefits below 49%, and require a reduction to around 31% once higher utilization is considered. The results show that the environmental benefits from EV adoption depend on a transition toward cleaner electricity generation.

title: Trade-Off ? What Trade-Off: Information Production without Illiquidity
affiliations: HEC Paris - Finance Department, University of Sussex Business School and University of Warwick - Warwick Business School

detail.title: Trade-Off ? What Trade-Off: Information Production without Illiquidity
detail.abstract: Private information in financial markets enhances the informational content of asset prices and thereby supports efficient resource allocation. Yet, informed traders extract rents at the expense of uninformed traders, generating a tradeoff between price informativeness and liquidity costs. Moreover, equilibrium investment in information acquisition may be socially excessive or insufficient. We show that a market structure separating the market for information from the market for liquidity can simultaneously deliver price informativeness, preserve liquidity, and align private incentives with efficient levels of information production.

title: Bluey! Markets, Money and Measurement
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin, Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU) and

detail.title: Bluey! Markets, Money and Measurement
detail.abstract: Since its 2018 debut, Bluey has become the most-streamed show in the world. Fueled by TikTok trends and viral short-form clips, Bluey has expanded beyond its original preschool demographic to become a Gen-Z sensation, driving massive spikes in viewership and engagement (Graterol, 2023). The show's broad appeal makes it unusually effective for teaching economics: its characters routinely make choices under constraints, and the resulting situations are humorous, emotionally resonant, and easy to discuss. The episodes are also brief, allowing instructors to illustrate key concepts without sacrificing class time. Building on Quinn et al. (2025), who demonstrated Bluey's value for introducing economic ideas to younger learners, we adapt the show for a university audience. We present three lessons using specific episodes to teach market efficiency and welfare ("Granny Mobile"), the circular flow of income ("Markets"), and GDP measurement ("Calypso").

title: Fairness Over Time: Impossibility, Institutional Cycling, and Housing Credit Algorithms
affiliations: Liberty University

detail.title: Fairness Over Time: Impossibility, Institutional Cycling, and Housing Credit Algorithms
detail.abstract:
Institutions governing algorithmic decision-making operate under temporally distributed accountability. Rules are selected before outcomes are known, evaluated once performance becomes observable, and reconsidered after long-run distributive trajectories emerge. This paper develops a theory of fairness as a temporal institutional problem rather than a static conflict among normative principles. Using a social-choice framework for algorithm selection in housing credit, the analysis formalizes three accountability constraints corresponding to distinct informational stages: exante symmetry, ex-post efficiency, and trajectory-based representation. The analysis establishes an impossibility result showing that no governance rule can satisfy all three constraints simultaneously across environments. The conflict arises not from disagreement over values but from governance operating under sequentially expanding information. Building on this result, the paper derives a corollary of institutional cycling: as new information becomes available, governance systems experience endogenous pressure to shift among fairness commitments. Institutions therefore do not converge on a stable fairness equilibrium but rotate among procedural, performance-based, and corrective orientations over time. Housing credit algorithms illustrate how these dynamics emerge in practice through recurring phases of procedural stabilization, efficiency evaluation, and representational response. The framework reframes algorithmic fairness as a problem of temporal accountability and institutional adaptation, suggesting that governance design should focus less on achieving final fairness solutions and more on managing predictable movement among competing constraints.

Author’s Note (Working Draft)

This paper began as a rethink of ideas that emerged during the review process for The Fairness Trilemma. The present version is an exploratory working draft focused on clarifying the temporal and institutional logic behind those ideas. It is shared in the spirit of open development; significant revision and formal tightening should be expected in subsequent versions.

title: Restricting Data Flows Is a Sign of Weakness
affiliations: University of Houston Law Center

detail.title: Restricting Data Flows Is a Sign of Weakness

declarations.funderStatement: Symposium, The Adolf A. Berle, Jr. Center on Corporations, Law & Society

detail.abstract:
There has been a seismic shift in American attitudes toward the free flow of data across borders. In less than a decade, the United States has transitioned from condemning barriers to digital trade to constructing a digital fortress of its own. It passed legislation that would effectively ban TikTok, a social media platform used by 170 million Americans, based on national security concerns stemming from its ties to China and associated risks of data surveillance and content manipulation. Upon legal challenge by TikTok on First Amendment grounds, the Supreme Court affirmed the ban’s constitutionality. Recent federal legislation and rulemaking likewise prohibit or restrict the transfer of sensitive personal data of U.S. persons to foreign adversary governments and entities under their control. 

This seismic shift may appear as a muscular regulatory flex domestically and a display of national strength internationally: The United States is invoking sovereignty as part of a tougher stance against its chief geopolitical rival, China. However, the opposite is true. Rather than demonstrating confidence, the protectionist turn is a sign of American vulnerability. It reveals deep-seated insecurities—if not an unintended admission that the United States is losing ground in a technological “great power competition.”

title: Private to Public: Deterrent Effects of Bans on Confidential Settlements
affiliations: University of Arkansas School of Law and Vanderbilt University - Law School

detail.title: Private to Public: Deterrent Effects of Bans on Confidential Settlements
detail.abstract: Nondisclosure agreements are common in settlement of legal disputes but are controversial as they suppress information that could prevent harm to others. But until the 2017 #MeToo movement, there had been little legislative effort to prohibit the practice in any context, and consequently no evidence on whether public disclosure of harms would be effective as a deterrent to wrongdoing. Following the #MeToo movement, more than ten states enacted bans on NDAs in settlement of employment discrimination claims. In addition to reputational harm to the employer, public airing of misconduct was expected to encourage other victims to come forward, which would have direct financial costs to the employer through litigation costs as well as in possible damages payments. We leverage variation in state legislation in timing and coverage to test the effects of these bans on employment discrimination court filings and outcomes in federal court, the most public forum for exposing acts as illegal. Supporting the prediction that bans could have a deterrent effect in the long term, we find an initial increase in filings, a decrease in settlement after filing, and an increase in the probability that the plaintiff prevails for cases without harassment allegations.

title: Reputation-Weighted Prediction Markets Under Wealth Heterogeneity and Heavy Tails
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Reputation-Weighted Prediction Markets Under Wealth Heterogeneity and Heavy Tails
detail.abstract: Capital-weighted prediction markets assume that willingness to stake capital proxies for information quality. This assumption fails whenever outcomes are heavy-tailed, private information is heterogeneous, and wealth does not positively correlate with forecasting skill-conditions that co-occur in cultural breakout markets and other fat-tailed domains. We propose a reputation-weighted aggregation mechanism that learns agent quality endogenously from demonstrated forecasting accuracy and modulates each agent's influence as the product of reputation and stake (wi = ri • si). Through Monte Carlo simulation under Pareto-distributed outcomes with heterogeneous private signals, we compare equal-weighted, capital-weighted, and reputation-weighted aggregation across three wealth-skill correlation regimes, parameter sweeps over tail heaviness and signal heterogeneity, and an inequality sensitivity sweep. Reputationweighted aggregation improves over capital-weighted aggregation in every tested configuration (p < 10-15 in main results), though the effect is modest (+0.13% to +0.20% in Brier score). Capitalweighting degrades forecasts by up to 5.27% under extreme wealth concentration with anti-correlated wealth and skill. The reputation correction grows with inequality, noise gap, and tail heaviness, but the multiplicative architecture is the binding constraint: a ∼10% learned reputation differential cannot override a 40× stake differential. The mechanism correctly identifies agent qualityreputation separation is invariant across all conditions-but lacks architectural authority to act proportionally on that knowledge. These findings motivate alternative weighting architectures that give demonstrated accuracy greater authority relative to raw capital. There is no tested configuration in which reputationweighting degrades performance.

title: Identifying and Supporting Strategic Net-Zero Transition Opportunities: The case of the EV Industry in South Africa
affiliations: Stellenbosch University, University of British Columbia (UBC) - School of Engineering and KU Leuven - Center for Economic Studies

detail.title: Identifying and Supporting Strategic Net-Zero Transition Opportunities: The case of the EV Industry in South Africa

declarations.ethicsApproval: The study obtained ethics approval from the relevant Stellenbosch University Research Ethics Committee.

detail.abstract: Vehicle production is a key industry in many countries. Electric vehicle (EV) adoption is regarded as key to reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Yet countries face challenges in transitioning to EV production. This places pressure on policymakers to balance industry needs and EV adoption. Supporting local EV production requires identifying activities with developmental potential and navigating the pathway to competitiveness. We propose a novel approach that identifies developmental activities that can leverage existing capabilities and determine the interventions required for competitiveness.

title: Reassessing Monetary Policy Effectiveness in Nigeria's Structural Economy
affiliations: Nigerian Institute of Social and Economic Research and Nigerian Institute of Social and Economic Research Ibadan Nigeria

detail.title: Reassessing Monetary Policy Effectiveness in Nigeria's Structural Economy
detail.abstract: This study reassesses the effectiveness of Nigeria’s Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) as a stabilization tool within a structurally constrained economy. The study adopts a qualitative analytical approach, synthesizing macroeconomic data, policy documents, and theoretical insights. Drawing on data from the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), and international sources covering 2015–2025, the analysis reveals that aggressive monetary tightening raising the MPR to 27.5% has had limited success in curbing inflation largely driven by supply-side shocks, exchange rate volatility, and fiscal imbalances. The findings show that while higher MPR levels help moderate demand-pull inflation, they simultaneously dampen GDP growth, reduce credit availability, and constrain real sector performance, particularly in agriculture and manufacturing. Empirical evidence and comparative global experiences indicate that the efficacy of MPR adjustments depends on complementary structural reforms, fiscal discipline, and institutional credibility. The paper concludes that coordinated fiscal monetary strategies, improved communication, and selective easing supported by structural and financial market reforms are essential for enhancing policy transmission, achieving macroeconomic stability, and fostering inclusive growth in Nigeria.

title: Who Clicks "Pay Later"? Financial Vulnerability and Buy Now Pay Later Usage
affiliations: and

detail.title: Who Clicks "Pay Later"? Financial Vulnerability and Buy Now Pay Later Usage
detail.abstract: As flexible, short-term, often interest-free Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) products become increasingly popular, this Insight reveals that individuals displaying certain characteristics of financial vulnerability are using BNPL to a greater extent, more frequently and simultaneously across multiple providers. These characteristics include a history of being refused credit elsewhere, being late on loan repayments previously, exhibiting low financial literacy, and overconfidence. While BNPL may be a convenient and affordable method to pay for products, our analysis highlights that it is being disproportionately used by those least equipped to manage the risks, raising concerns about debt accumulation. This underlines the importance of clear disclosures designed with behavioural insights in mind and the implementation of credit checks by providers that take into account total financial commitments by prospective borrowers.

title: Powering Digital Mega-loads: Barriers and Solutions to Accelerate Grid Efficiency, Investment and GDP Growth in the AI Era
affiliations: University of London - Birkbeck College and University of Bath

detail.title: Powering Digital Mega-loads: Barriers and Solutions to Accelerate Grid Efficiency, Investment and GDP Growth in the AI Era
detail.abstract: This paper examines how rapid growth in data centre demand interacts with electricity systems that are already facing capacity constraints, decarbonisation pressures and heightened political scrutiny. Focusing on data centres as large-load customers, we distinguish them from both small loads and generation assets to highlight the relevant issues accordingly. Drawing on international literature and case studies from Europe and North America, we identify five systemic barriers to timely and efficient data centre integration: long times to connect; cost uncertainty for both developers and utilities; contested grid cost allocation; capacity constraints; and local political and community opposition. For each barrier, we evaluate emerging regulatory and contractual responses, including deep versus shallow charging regimes, upfront fees and contractual safeguards, flexible and non-firm connections, bespoke large-load tariffs, bring-your-own-generation (BYOG) requirements, location incentives, and socio-environmental and economic-impact criteria. We show that these instruments operate through a limited set of underlying channels and that many can address multiple barriers simultaneously. We argue that fairness concepts in connection policy may need to evolve from strict procedural equality towards outcomes that also reflect net-zero, reliability and economic-development objectives. The paper concludes by outlining how regulators, system operators, planners and data centre developers can use the proposed framework as a diagnostic and design tool, and highlights priorities for future empirical research on policy effectiveness, load-flexibility behaviour and long-term community and system impacts.

title: Structural Anti-Money Laundering Enforcement Via Ternary Logic: A Governance-Grade Specification

detail.title: Structural Anti-Money Laundering Enforcement Via Ternary Logic: A Governance-Grade Specification
detail.abstract: The global Anti-Money Laundering (AML) framework currently operates on a bivalent (binary) logic of "Allow" or "Deny," creating a structural inability to manage economic actions under epistemic uncertainty. This architecture forces high-ambiguity transactions into a permissive state to maintain liquidity, resulting in an "interdiction gap" where illicit funds are identified only after settlement via post-hoc Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs). This paper proposes Ternary Logic (TL), a triadic state-machine architecture (+1 Proceed, 0 Epistemic Hold,-1 Refuse) that enforces "No Log = No Action" constraints at the protocol level. We define the Epistemic Hold as a deterministic, time-bounded state that converts unbounded probabilistic regulatory risk into bounded, measurable latency. The technical specification introduces a Dual-Lane Latency architecture to decouple inference (≤2ms) from cryptographic anchoring (≤500ms), and utilizes Merkle-batched anchoring to achieve O(1) verification complexity per batch. Case studies, including a "Red Team" Hold Flood attack simulation, demonstrate how dynamic evidence thresholds and Verifiable Delay Functions (VDFs) allow the system to "fail closed" under adversarial load, preserving systemic integrity.

title: The Impact of AI Evaluators and Incentive Schemes on Employee Idea Sharing
affiliations: Tulane University - A.B. Freeman School of Business, A.B. Freeman School of Business at Tulane, Texas State University and Eller College of Management, University of Arizona

detail.title: The Impact of AI Evaluators and Incentive Schemes on Employee Idea Sharing
detail.abstract: We study how creative idea sharing is impacted when AI programs evaluate employees' ideas under different incentive schemes. In a controlled experiment with a two-by-two design, we manipulate the evaluator (AI versus human) and the incentive scheme (piece-rate versus tournament-style). In line with our theoretical predictions, participants submit significantly more ideas under AI evaluation than human evaluation when incentives are piece-rate, but not when incentives are tournament-style. We also find that AI evaluation is associated with higher average idea quality, with a disproportionately large share of the highest-quality ideas arising when AI-based evaluation is combined with piece-rate incentives. This quality increase is driven primarily by greater usefulness of the submitted ideas. Together, these findings have important implications for managers because they suggest that AI evaluators can help managers scale the evaluation of creative ideas while increasing both the quantity and quality of employee-generated creative output.

title: Dissecting Inconsistencies in Corporate Disclosures: Evidence from Public and Private Earnings Calls
affiliations: , The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences and The University of Hong Kong, Faculty of Business and Economics

detail.title: Dissecting Inconsistencies in Corporate Disclosures: Evidence from Public and Private Earnings Calls
detail.abstract: We employ a novel dataset comprising public and private earnings call transcripts for listed firms in China. We construct a comprehensive topic taxonomy to dissect disclosure inconsistencies by firm managers across public and private meetings. Our analysis reveals that managers introduce a non-trivial proportion of new, and often material, topics in private meetings. They also demonstrate distinct narrative styles and vocal delivery strategies when addressing the same topics at different meetings. We find that these disclosure inconsistencies are associated with meeting-, manager- and firm-level characteristics. We further examine the informativeness of disclosure inconsistencies and show that these measures are predictive of firms’ future stock returns and illiquidity. Our findings highlight the managers’ inconsistent disclosure behaviors across meetings and their adverse implications for a level playing field in the capital market.

title: The Opportunity Cost of Homogeneity: An Econometric Exploration of Demographic Diversity in Innovation
affiliations: Colorado College - Department of Economics and Business and Colorado College

detail.title: The Opportunity Cost of Homogeneity: An Econometric Exploration of Demographic Diversity in Innovation

declarations.funderStatement: Colorado College's Natalie Gubbay Fund for Endowed Student Research

detail.abstract: Despite evidence suggesting that diverse perspectives are highly beneficial to creative fields, it is challenging to assess even the compositional diversity of patent inventors because the U.S. Patent Office does not collect demographic information from patent applicants. We adapt Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding (BISG) to infer likely intersectional demographic identities of listed inventors, with multiple validity tests to ensure accuracy. After describing the patterns of (non)diversity over time, space, industry and technology type, we model the outcomes of diversity (e.g. various metrics of patent value). We develop a completely new measure of patent novelty using AI-informed semantic analysis in order to eliminate citation bias in valuations, finding a strong and persistent relationship between all forms of compositional diversity and patent novelty.

title: Field-Shi (FS) Framework: Multi-Field Rule Dynamics, Phase Transitions, and Existential Games in Complex Socio-Technical Systems
affiliations: Nanyang Technological University (NTU)

detail.title: Field-Shi (FS) Framework: Multi-Field Rule Dynamics, Phase Transitions, and Existential Games in Complex Socio-Technical Systems

keywords: A Semi-Formal Strategic Grammar Beyond Probability

detail.abstract:
The structural instability of modern complex socio-technical systems is increasingly difficult to explain solely through probability theory, causal inference, or classical game theory. These analytical tools typically presuppose a relatively stable rule environment, gradual structural evolution, and exogenously given game rules. In practice, however, many systemic risks do not arise from local misjudgments or isolated decision errors. Rather, they emerge from transformations at the rule layer, nonlinear amplification across interacting domains, and structural phase transitions that reconfigure the system itself.

This paper proposes the Field–Shi (FS) framework as a semi-formal analytical grammar for understanding multi-field rule dynamics. Within this framework, a complex system is represented as a constellation of interacting fields, each governed by its own rule set, resource configuration, and settlement mechanism. Actions within a field generate directional and gradient-like Shi, understood as structured potential that shapes the amplification, suppression, or redirection of effects. System-level behavior is not reducible to isolated outcomes within a single field; instead, it results from the configuration of cross-field couplings and from the processes through which Shi is generated, transferred, accumulated, or dissipated.

A system’s state can thus be described as a structured composition of multiple fields, each with its own dynamic distribution of Shi, together with a coupling architecture that links them. When gradients of Shi intensify and cross critical thresholds, structural phase transitions may occur. Such transitions can manifest as rule rewriting, field substitution, institutional reconfiguration, or degradation of structural coherence.

The core contributions of the FS framework are fivefold. First, it proposes a minimum first-principles grammar for rule-layer dynamics. Second, it constructs a coherent inference chain that connects rule formation, coupling deepening, and phase transition. Third, it establishes a typology of system collapse based on Root-layer parameters, distinguishing between reversible disruptions and structural breakdown. Fourth, it introduces an Existential Game model that differentiates ordinary failure from situations in which Subject-Variables become structurally captured by the very systems they helped create. Fifth, it positions FS as a Strategic Cognition Layer within the AI technology stack, providing a structural interface for evaluating rule stability, coupling risk, and long-term alignment constraints.

FS does not replace probability theory, causal modeling, or game-theoretic analysis. Rather, it reorganizes their scope within a higher-order structural perspective. By shifting the focus from optimization under fixed rules to the dynamics of rule evolution, consolidation, and collapse, the framework offers a way to analyze how complex systems transform over time—and how subjects may preserve actionability in environments where the rules themselves are in flux.

title: Cursed by the Algorithm: Cue-Triggered Consumption and Platform Recommendation
affiliations: Cornell University - Cornell University, College of Computing and Information Science (CIS), Department of Information Science, Students

detail.title: Cursed by the Algorithm: Cue-Triggered Consumption and Platform Recommendation
detail.abstract: I develop a dynamic model of engagement-driven recommendation in which a monopolist platform chooses feed composition while users allocate a finite attention budget across offline time and multiple content categories. Users may enter a cuetriggered ("hot") state in which triggering content is overvalued relative to deliberative ("cold") preferences, generating a wedge between engagement and welfare. When the platform updates recommendations to maximize observed engagement, it optimally responds to this wedge but does not internalize the cumulative harm from repeated exposure. I characterize a cursed equilibrium in which personalization endogenously concentrates the feed on triggering categories for vulnerable users, reinforcing myopic consumption and creating a self-reinforcing loop that can culminate in temporary or permanent disengagement. The discrete formulation enables analysis of integer-valued policy interventions-content caps, diversity requirements, and category floors-that have no natural continuous analog. I connect these instruments to the emerging regulatory landscape, showing that type-blind structural constraints on feed composition can improve welfare without requiring the regulator to identify vulnerable users or classify content.

title: The Political Ecology of Recovery from Armed Conflict: The Case of Landmines in Mozambique
affiliations: , Indiana University and Indiana University

detail.title: The Political Ecology of Recovery from Armed Conflict: The Case of Landmines in Mozambique
detail.abstract: The devastation wrought by landmines on local populations is well known. However the broader effects of mine presence on postwar recovery, and the progress of a 'peace process', remain largely unexamined. Both the academic and practitioner literature regarding landmines lack a framework within which the mix of economic, political, social, agricultural, and ecologic repercussions of mine presence in a context of postwar recovery can be investigated. Here we consider the utility of political ecology to examine the influence of landmine presence on the socioecological relations important to postwar recovery in Mozambique. Landmines constitute the primary obstacle to reconstruction and development in Mozambique. Because mine presence influences different aspects of recovery differently, we have selected three cases in the country where mine presence has impacted important components of recovery: agriculture, transportation corridors, and international investment. Peace process and recovery efforts by the international community do not presently address the broader, non-medical influences of landmine presence on recovery, and it is the intention of this article to contribute to an initial examination of these issues.

title: The Missing Link: "Credible Scarcity" and Unpleasant Monetarist Arithmetic

detail.title: The Missing Link: "Credible Scarcity" and Unpleasant Monetarist Arithmetic
detail.abstract: A central riddle in monetary economics is fiscal dominance: why can a central bank lose control of inflation when fiscal backing is weak, even if it is formally independent and committed to price stability? Classic "unpleasant monetarist arithmetic" shows that government financing needs can eventually force money creation, but it leaves open a practical question: how, exactly, does the nominal anchor stop working in the economy? This paper proposes a new theory of the anchor based on a simple idea. Money is valuable only if people believe it will remain hard to create or replicate in the future. In reality, that hardness is not automatic: it is produced by enforcement-laws, procedures, payment infrastructure, and verification-and it can become unreliable during fiscal stress, when exceptions and overrides are more likely. I model this by introducing an economy-wide measure of how reliably monetary scarcity is enforced over time (I call it scarcity enforcement). Scarcity enforcement affects the real cost and reliability of using money in trade, and therefore affects its value; at the same time, the value of money affects the incentives to maintain or relax enforcement. This creates a feedback loop between beliefs, enforcement, and value. The main result is a sharp stability criterion. If scarcity enforcement is sufficiently predictable, the feedback loop stabilizes beliefs and money has a unique, well-anchored value. If enforcement is sufficiently uncertain, the loop no longer stabilizes beliefs, and self-fulfilling swings in value become possible. Fiscal stress matters because it increases the likelihood and unpredictability of exceptions to enforcement, pushing the economy into the unstable region where the anchor fails endogenously. The framework yields clear implications for institutional design: maintaining monetary stability requires rules and institutions that allow necessary fiscal action while keeping the enforcement of scarcity reliable in stress states.

title: Noise Law
affiliations: Pace University - School of Law

detail.title: Noise Law

publicationDetails.detailsText: Michigan Journal of Environmental & Administrative Law, 0[10.36640/mjeal.15.1.noise]

detail.abstract:
The rumble of traffic, the drone of air conditioners, the blast of construction equipment. These are the mundane sources of noise pollution that we all experience but rarely think about. Or, if we do think about noise pollution, we don’t think of it as a central piece of federal environmental law. This Article, however, demonstrates that noise law is, or was, central to American environmental law, and it offers insights into how environmental protection and administrative governance work today.

In the 1970s, during the height of environmental activism and policymaking, lawmakers recognized noise as a serious pollutant alongside issues we continue to discuss today, such as dirty air, contaminated water, and biodiversity loss. The federal government built an impressive framework to tackle the problem, complete with science-based mandates, dynamic regulatory authority, and citizen suit provisions.

But then something remarkable happened: it quietly fell apart. Through presidential neglect and civil society inattention, the fledgling noise control system collapsed. This Article shows exactly how this happened, revealing the political and administrative forces that can make or break regulatory programs.

Three key components of noise law distinguish it from other environmental issues. First, by one line of thinking, noise pollution really isn’t “pollution” because noise waves are not tangible like particles and toxins, both of which trigger greater disgust reactions and sustain public attention. Second, Congress created fragmented control over noise governance, giving the Environmental Protection Agency supervisory authority but lodging important authorities within agencies across the federal government. Third, noise does not travel as far as many other pollutants and it does not accumulate in the environment or bodies, making it easier to escape—spatially and temporally—for those with the political and economic power to do so. This last component makes noise an especially acute example of an environmental injustice, which may also make it an especially easy problem for elites to overlook.

Ultimately, this Article demonstrates that noise law serves as a revealing case study for understanding environmental policy and administrative governance broadly. Noise law offers insights into the dynamics of regulatory decline, the politics of environmental justice, and the difficulties of structuring administrative systems for complex public problems.

title: Work from Home and Fertility
affiliations: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, Instituto Tecnológico Autónomo de México (ITAM), Stanford University - Department of Economics, Stanford University, Stanford University, Ifo Institute and Princeton University

detail.title: Work from Home and Fertility
detail.abstract: We investigate how fertility relates to work from home (WFH) in the post-pandemic era, drawing on original data from our Global Survey of Working Arrangements and U.S. Survey of Working Arrangements and Attitudes. Realized fertility from 2023 to 2025 and future planned fertility are higher among adults who WFH at least one day a week and, for couples, higher yet when both partners do so. Estimated lifetime fertility is greater by 0.32 children per woman when both partners WFH one or more days per week as compared to the case where neither does. The implications for national fertility rates differ across countries due mainly to large differences in WFH rates. In a complementary analysis using other U.S. data before and after the pandemic, one-year fertility rates rise with WFH opportunities in one’s own occupation and, for couples, in the partner’s occupation.

title: Public Policy, Institutional Quality, and Sustainable Development: Evidence from Nigeria and Sub-Saharan African
affiliations: University of Cross River State, University of Cross River State and University of Cross River State (UNICROSS) Calabar Nigeria

detail.title: Public Policy, Institutional Quality, and Sustainable Development: Evidence from Nigeria and Sub-Saharan African

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is no personal or finacial involument of any agent to the tune of the work, only taking a wholistic view of contributing to the body of knownledge in the region.

detail.abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive empirical and analytical examination of the relationship between public policy, institutional quality, and sustainable development in Nigeria and the broader Sub-Saharan African (SSA) region. Anchored in institutional economics and contemporary development theory, the study conceptualizes institutional quality as a critical mediating mechanism through which public policies are formulated, implemented, and ultimately translated into sustainable development outcomes. Utilizing secondary data drawn from internationally recognized sources including the World Governance Indicators, World Development Indicators, Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) databases, and selected regional governance reports the paper adopts a comparative and integrative analytical framework that enables both cross-country assessment and context-specific interpretation. Nigeria is examined as a focal case within the SSA region, allowing for nuanced institutional insights while preserving regional comparability. The analysis reveals that systematic variations in political stability, regulatory quality, rule of law, control of corruption, and government effectiveness significantly account for observed disparities in economic growth trajectories, social welfare provisioning, and environmental sustainability across SSA countries. Empirical evidence further indicates that states characterized by stronger and more coherent institutional frameworks are better positioned to convert public policy commitments into measurable development gains, whereas weak institutional environments undermine policy credibility, intensify socio-economic inequality, and weaken environmental governance. The paper concludes that institutional strengthening remains indispensable for achieving inclusive and sustainable development in Nigeria and SSA, and it advances policy relevant recommendations emphasizing governance reform, accountability enhancement, institutional capacity building, and policy coherence as foundational pathways toward the attainment of the Sustainable Development Goals

title: Land Dispute Resolution in Mozambique: Evidence and Institutions of Agroforestry Technology Adoption

detail.title: Land Dispute Resolution in Mozambique: Evidence and Institutions of Agroforestry Technology Adoption
detail.abstract: Successful adoption of natural resource management technologies requires that important fundamentals of property rights be significantly established.  Because disputes over property rights occur universally, the ability to successfully defend one’s rights to property exercises a central influence on the tenure security necessary for technology adoption. However defending rights to property rests upon the possession of evidence significantly available, and widely regarded as legitimate.  This chapter presents work carried out in postwar Mozambique on the availability and legitimacy of evidence pertaining to land tenure dispute resolution. What is unusual about the Mozambique case is that the physical presence of a natural resource management technology, agroforestry trees in this case, also serves as one of the most widely available and legitimate forms of evidence in the postwar period.  Such an arrangement reveals important aspects about the reverse relationship between property rights and technology adoption. While such an evidence role for a technology at first may appear to encourage further adoption of agroforestry, important influences on property rights in the postwar setting serve to discourage full adoption, and jeopardize the long-term presence of existing agroforestry trees.  It remains to be seen if recent legislative changes regarding property rights will successfully engage customary forms of evidence and encourage full adoption of agroforestry in Mozambique.

title: From Walls to Law: An Ethnographic Journey on Street Art, Graffiti and Copyright
affiliations: City University London, The City Law School

detail.title: From Walls to Law: An Ethnographic Journey on Street Art, Graffiti and Copyright
detail.abstract: This paper traces an ethnographic journey from London's streets to contemporary legal and policy debates, showing how immersive engagement with street art and graffiti communities can reshape understandings of copyright, public scholarship, and the role of legal academics. Drawing on long-term fieldwork, interviews, and participatory observation across several cities in the world, it documents how embedded legal expertise can both elucidate the gap between copyright theory and artists' lived experiences and help artists resist exploitative appropriations of their work. The article argues that publicly engaged legal research, grounded in reciprocity and co-creation, can influence judicial reasoning, urban policy, and teaching practice while advancing social justice in the regulation of urban creative expression.

title: Estimating the Demand for Walkable Neighborhoods: Evidence from a City-Wide Zoning Reform in Miami, FL
affiliations: West Virginia University - College of Business & Economics

detail.title: Estimating the Demand for Walkable Neighborhoods: Evidence from a City-Wide Zoning Reform in Miami, FL
detail.abstract: This paper estimates household demand for walkable neighborhoods in Miami following the city's zoning reform to increase walkability. I construct a behaviorally grounded walkability measure that integrates residents' observed 15-minute walking behavior with a CES-style price index capturing the richness and affordability of nearby amenities. Using smartphone mobility data, I show that baseline patterns reveal strong local activity-on average, 30.3 % of essential visits occur locally-and that greater local access significantly increases realized neighborhood usage and generates more frequent trip chains. A structural discrete-choice model reveals that households have a strong preference for walkability and are willing to pay about $24 per square foot for a one-standard-deviation increase in walkability. The results suggest that land-use reform and housing supply policy can meaningfully influence urban accessibility by enabling denser, mixed-use development consistent with revealed household preferences.

title: Reclaiming Work-Spreading: The Forgotten Purpose of the Fair Labor Standards Act

detail.title: Reclaiming Work-Spreading: The Forgotten Purpose of the Fair Labor Standards Act
detail.abstract:
Americans face multiple crises of work. The bottom half of the wage distribution suffers from widespread un- and underemployment, while the top half works ever more hours. All workers are potentially subject to a new wave of displacement by artificial intelligence. Existing policies, such as job creation and income redistribution, have failed to resolve these crises. But there is an alternative policy that is at once more radical and more realistic: the spreading of work across the population through hours regulation.

The United States already possesses a legal regime that implements work-spreading. The overtime provision of the Depression-era Fair Labor Standards Act was intended to spread work from the overworked to the unemployed by placing a financial disincentive on hours over forty. Unfortunately, recent court cases have undermined this regime. In the last decade, the federal judiciary has repeatedly foreclosed the extension of overtime protection to white-collar workers. These decisions have limited the number of hours available to be spread, rendering work-spreading all but impossible. 

It is not just the judiciary. Spreading work today will require substantial changes: the narrowing of the white-collar exemption, the strengthening of overtime law, and the reimagining of work. And yet, as a policy uniquely suited to address today’s shortage of work and lopsided labor market, work-spreading is worth reclaiming.

title: Macro News in Market Moves: Classifying News through Asset Co-movements
affiliations: Bank of Canada, Bank of Canada and Government of Canada - Bank of Canada

detail.title: Macro News in Market Moves: Classifying News through Asset Co-movements
detail.abstract: This paper introduces CLONE (Classification Of News), a method that decomposes asset price movements into four types of macroeconomic news-aggregate demand, productivity, inflation, and monetary policy-based on joint changes in prices of stocks, bonds, and inflation swaps. CLONE's simplicity and forward-looking focus enable the identification of real-time economic signals that are critical for understanding market behavior and guiding policy decisions. We show that from 2004 to 2024 aggregate demand news historically dominated daily variation in asset prices, while inflation and monetary policy news have gained importance since 2021. We validate our method against sign-restricted VAR models and apply it to major U.S. macroeconomic data releases, providing insights into how market participants interpret and react to forward-looking information. We discuss several benefits of our approach relative to the standard sign restriction method.

title: The Changing Value of Employment
affiliations: Vancouver School of Economics, UBC and Université de Montréal, Dept. of Economics

detail.title: The Changing Value of Employment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare

detail.abstract: Are earnings informative about the returns from work? We estimate the value of worker-occupation matches in an equilibrium model that distinguishes between wages and latent returns and derive a measure of rents that has three properties: (i) it reflects wages and unobserved match values; (ii) it delivers a monetary metric for compensating differentials; (iii) it illustrates how the marginal workers within a match affect the rents of others. We show that earnings closely track rents between 1980 and 2018. The results highlight a dichotomy: while rents arise from latent values, their evolution is driven by technology.

title: Tokens All the Way Down: A Money View of Decentralized Finance

detail.title: Tokens All the Way Down: A Money View of Decentralized Finance
detail.abstract: We apply the Money View framework to Decentralized Finance (DeFi), constructing a Token Graph that maps the ecosystem as a layered credit hierarchy. Using a balance-sheet model-treating each nontrading protocol's input-output relationship as a derivation edge-we algorithmically discover 169 base tokens and assign hierarchy tiers from pool-level data across 7,000 protocols. The layering multipliertotal claims per dollar of base assets-declined from 3.6 × to 2.1 × during the 2022-2024 crises before rising to 4.7 × by late 2025, with lending (45%) and staking (38%) accounting for over 80% of excess layering. Panel regressions on 2.0 million pool-month observations reveal two opposing yield channels. The discrete tier coefficient is negative,-0.52 pp, 𝑝 = 0.06, reflecting systematic omission of upstream returns at deeper tiers; an embedded yield correction attenuates this by 93%. Graph distance-integer hops to the nearest base token-carries a robust negative coefficient of-1.86 pp per hop, 𝑝 < 0.001, that survives the embedded yield correction with only 23% attenuation, confirming a structural distance discount. In a joint model on corrected APY, both channels are significant: a compositional tier premium of +2.0 pp, 𝑝 < 0.001, and a structural distance discount of-2.9 pp per hop, 𝑝 < 0.001.

title: The Market Theology of the Early Church: Some Theological Contributions to the Dismal Science
affiliations: Grove City College

detail.title: The Market Theology of the Early Church: Some Theological Contributions to the Dismal Science
detail.abstract: This Article seeks to make three modest contributions. First, this Article serves to correct a failed historiography of the early church. While no patristic scholar argues that the early church professed a sort of proto-communism, other disciplines, namely, economics and business, perpetuate a misapprehension of how the early church thought about property and markets. Second, this Article offers an intellectual survey of both Ante-Nicaean and Nicaean/Post-Nicaean church fathers on property and markets. Through this survey, this Article seeks to demonstrate a general theme of the acceptance of private property, capital accumulation, market exchange, and arbitrage. Finally, this Article supports two theoretical contributions to business ethics from the fathers: property is a moral instrument where ownership confers normative obligations, rather than absolute entitlements; and moral formation and voluntary distribution are ethically preferable to coercive redistribution through regulation. This Article concludes with three practical contributions to business ethics from the fathers.

title: AppleCare or Not? The Math Behind Warranties, Self-Insurance, and Risk By Ishan Gupta
affiliations: Indiana University Bloomington

detail.title: AppleCare or Not? The Math Behind Warranties, Self-Insurance, and Risk By Ishan Gupta
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the economics of AppleCare+, Apple's extended warranty program, using an expected value framework and Monte Carlo simulations. By comparing AppleCare+ to self-insurance across different user profiles, we show how outcomes vary depending on risk type and usage behavior. For low-risk users, AppleCare+ is not actuarially fair, while high-risk users may benefit significantly. The findings have implications for consumers, regulators, and third-party insurers. The study highlights the broader role of extended warranties in risk pooling, consumer protection, and corporate strategy.

title: Multi-Sector Capacity Building

detail.title: Multi-Sector Capacity Building
detail.abstract: In a variety of conflict-affected countries revenue from high-value natural resources—oil, natural gas, minerals, gemstones, timber, and others—are an important segment of the economy and provide a good amount of money to state budgets (Badeeb et al., 2017; Bruch et al., 2011). While well managed high-value natural resources can be important in financing recovery, and development, when mismanaged, money from such resources can weaken economies and governments, and greatly increase the risk of violence in what are known as variations of the “resource curse” (e.g., Sexton, 2019; Murshed, 2018; Badeeb et al., 2017; Paine, 2016; Alao, 2007; Cabrales and Hauk, 2010; Karabegović, 2009; Lujala and Rustad, 2012). Recent findings have highlighted linkages between the resource curse and armed conflicts (Ross, 2018).

title: Artificial Intelligence Investments and Expertise Erosion
affiliations: Queen's University and Queen's University - Smith School of Business

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence Investments and Expertise Erosion
detail.abstract: We study the feedback between automation and expertise accumulation. Building on Autor and Thompson's (2025) "expertise framework", we develop an overlapping generations model with endogenous on-the-job learning. Automation reduces learning in entry-level tasks, slowing expertise acquisition and worsening the economy's expertise distribution. Yet, we show that pre-existing automation decreases firms' willingness to pay for marginal improvements in automation. Indeed, these improvements benefit occupations requiring high human expertise, while the supply of workers with high expertise declines with prior automation. This weakens the dynamic complementarity between automation and expertise-substituting technologies.

title: Land Policy Reform, Customary Rule of Law and the Peace Process in Sierra Leone

detail.title: Land Policy Reform, Customary Rule of Law and the Peace Process in Sierra Leone
detail.abstract: Armed conflict is particularly destructive to socio-legal relations regarding land and property. Reconstruction priorities increasingly include land and property legislative reform as part of efforts to address the causes and reasons for continuation of conflicts. However, a pervasive problem is that postwar laws are extremely difficult to connect with informal on-the-ground developments regarding perceptions of spatially-based rights; as populations pursue livelihoods, grievances, and aspirations. Left unattended, the problem constitutes a potential flashpoint for a return to conflict. This article examines this connection for postwar Sierra Leone, in order to highlight issues and questions of potential utility. The stakes are high for successfully connecting postwar land tenure laws with informal socio-legal realities. For Sierra Leone a primary issue is the presence of a large population without access to land, tenure insecurity discouraging investment, and large-scale food insecurity and rural unemployment while a great deal of arable and previously cultivated land stands idle.

title: Under the Mandate of Heaven: A Historical Study of Omens and Executives
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Sungkyunkwan University and Sungkyunkwan University

detail.title: Under the Mandate of Heaven: A Historical Study of Omens and Executives
detail.abstract: In this paper, we explore extraordinary natural occurrences as omens and their historical influence on legitimacy concerns. Natural disasters and anomalies have long been interpreted as divine interventions to challenge the legitimacy of the ruling body. In order to understand how ruling executives responded to these challenges, we utilize the Veritable Records of the Joseon Dynasty of Korea, the official daily accounts of the kingdom’s various affairs recorded between 1413 and 1865 CE. Covering the longest continual period of a dynasty known in the world, the annals document daily decisions made by the rulers and their councils. Under Joseon’s Confucian belief system, they also record in detail various extraordinary natural phenomena as omens signaling weakened legitimacy. We find that the omens provided both performance and belief-based legitimacy shocks to the royal court, and led to meaningful changes in how the executives made decisions.

title: An Acacia Based Design for Sustainable Livestock Carrying Capacity on Irrigated Farmlands in Semi-Arid Africa

detail.title: An Acacia Based Design for Sustainable Livestock Carrying Capacity on Irrigated Farmlands in Semi-Arid Africa
detail.abstract: Multiple land use designs are becoming increasingly necessary in semi-arid Africa as growing populations focus numerous production systems onto spatially limited arable lands. Engineering distinct land uses into a single area ideally requires that land use components compliment each other, and operate in predictable magnitudes. Quantitative evaluations of components to be included in multiple land use designs are necessary to determine both how components would 'fit' together, and how these would serve populations participating in distinct production systems. With data gathered in Somalia, this study considers a design in which fodder producing trees and irrigated agriculture could be integrated. Following a discussion of the benefits of such an integration, this analysis focuses on a quantitative examination of potential livestock carrying capacity from Acacia albida trees in an irrigated area. Comparisons are made with observed livestock numbers in order to determine if such a design could accommodate the seasonal influx of nomadic herds. The land use elements that comprise carrying capacity are themselves examined to see which elements might be managed to offset or take advantage of those which are not easily managed.

title: R&D Strategies of Polluting Firms Facing an Emissions Tax: Cost Reduction Versus Pollution Abatement
affiliations: Okayama University, Illinois State University - Department of Economics and

detail.title: R&D Strategies of Polluting Firms Facing an Emissions Tax: Cost Reduction Versus Pollution Abatement
detail.abstract: Firms’ efforts to reduce pollution emissions in their production processes are induced by market forces as well as governmental regulatory instruments. The market forces, which might induce firms to increase production to maximize profits, work at cross-purposes. One of the common solutions is that firms resort to R&D investment, which lowers production costs with greater pollution being an unwelcome by-product　(the tax burden effect). Pollution abatement (PA) investment, which is another solution, focuses on reducing emissions, with no direct impacts on production costs. We evaluate whether R&D investment effectively plays a role in profit maximization depends on the tax burden effect. Besides, judging from a socio-economic perspective, the PA strategy is significantly superior to the R&D strategy when (pollution) damage cost parameters are medium or high. However, the reverse result holds when they are small. Our findings thus formally flesh out the implications of choosing R&D versus PA strategies in response to pollution control regulations.

title: Nomadic Pastoralism and Irrigated Agriculture in Somalia: Utilization of Existing Land Use Patterns in Designs for Multiple Access of "High Potential" Areas of Semi-Arid Africa

detail.title: Nomadic Pastoralism and Irrigated Agriculture in Somalia: Utilization of Existing Land Use Patterns in Designs for Multiple Access of "High Potential" Areas of Semi-Arid Africa
detail.abstract: The persistent interplay of food production problems, land degradation, and social and climatic difficulties on the Horn of Africa result in recurring famines in spite of vast sums of money spent on agricultural development. As land resources-which undergird both social and production systems in Africa-become increasingly degraded, development efforts, especially in problematic areas, need to become part of comprehensive resource use programs that take into account the existing regional land use ecology. Designs which disrupt the ecology of established land uses can lead to extensive degradation because such uses are linked to wider areas; and the effects of such disruption can ultimately threaten the viability of the proposed schemes themselves. While African agriculture has traditionally met greater food needs by expanding the area under cultivation and irrigation, the increasing scarcity of new high quality arable land means that multiple use of "high potential" areas will become a priority. This paper describes a multiple land use in a "high potential" river basin of Somalia, in the context of the existing use patterns involved in irrigated agriculture and nomadic pastoralism. The spatial and temporal access and use of resources are analyzed, and recommendations made for improving the integration of these production systems.

title: The Role of 'Critical Resource' Tenure in the Post-Conflict Recovery of African Agriculture: the Case of Southern Somalia

detail.title: The Role of 'Critical Resource' Tenure in the Post-Conflict Recovery of African Agriculture: the Case of Southern Somalia
detail.abstract: Large scale dislocation of African populations due to conflict and famine will have profound impacts on future agricultural potential and security over large areas. The disruption of resource use and access arrangements for large numbers of rural inhabitants compromises rational use of resources and the productive capacity of these. Post-conflict recovery of many subsistence producers will begin with a dependence on locations where fertile land, perennial water supplies, infrastructure, and refugee services can be utilized-especially where these exist within the more arid parts of the continent. In Somalia, reliance on such spatially limited 'critical resource' areas in the course of recovery will take place as competing claims are made on valuable resources, and participants in different modes of resource use are concentrated into these areas. These, together with land degradation, and periodic drought, will affect rates of recovery for individuals, households and production systems-with repercussions on the productivity of land resources. The formation and efficacy of tenure dispute resolution mechanisms will play a large role in the utilization of critical resource areas for recovery, as well as for future tenure security and food security. Development and rehabilitation efforts can embrace the emerging amalgam of local notions concerning dispute resolution, tenure security, and land use, in the implementation of 'recovery tenure' arrangements for critical resource areas. Such arrangements might subsequently be considered in the construction of a national tenure system.

title: Pastoralist Resource Use and Access in Somalia: A Changing Context of Development, Environmental Stress, and Conflict

detail.title: Pastoralist Resource Use and Access in Somalia: A Changing Context of Development, Environmental Stress, and Conflict
detail.abstract: Act on pastoralists and livestock herding activities. Over half of the estimated 8.4 million Somalis are nomadic or semi-nomadic herders subject to the vagaries of an arid climate. Pastoralism is the most important agricultural enterprise in the country and will continue to be the basis for food production for future populations (Conze and Labahn 1986:15; Handulle and Gay 1987:36; Markakis 1993:9; Unruh 1993a:308; Lewis 1975:1). title: The Sequencing of Import Tariffs and Emissions Taxes: Does the Timing Impact Economic Performance?
affiliations: Illinois State University - Department of Economics and Chuo University

detail.title: The Sequencing of Import Tariffs and Emissions Taxes: Does the Timing Impact Economic Performance?
detail.abstract: The intersection of environmental policies and trade policies on external diseconomies has received considerable attention in recent years. However, the impacts of the timing of pollution taxes versus import tariffs on economic performance have not been formally considered, and this forms the focus of this work. In a political economy context, import tariffs might be imposed first due to protectionist or budgetary considerations, while environmental compulsions might lead to precedence of pollution taxes. Our results show that social welfare is greater when import tariffs precede pollution taxes. Pollution taxes are lower, and domestic production is greater when import tariffs are imposed first.

title: Integration Of Transhumant Pastoralism And Irrigated Agriculture

detail.title: Integration Of Transhumant Pastoralism And Irrigated Agriculture
detail.abstract: Agricultural development projects in the fertile and most well watered areas of arid and semiarid Africa usually deny access to nomadic pastoralists whose production system and livelihood depend upon such areas in the dry season and during frequent droughts. The result can be degradation of range resources through overgrazing, and greater vulnerability of pastoralists. Recent calls for "compatible" land use schemes or "nonexclusionary" agricultural development projects in the context of pastoralist transhumance, suggest allowing pastoralists structured access to project sites in the dry season in order to utilize forage and water supplies. This paper examines the capacity of an irrigation scheme to support the seasonal influx of transhumant livestock in dry seasons of varying severity. The livestock carrying capacity of the existing mosaic of land use patterns and practices is used in the determination of the proportional areas of land use needed to absorb large seasonal concentrations of livestock.

title: Multi-Horizon Machine Learning Forecasts of Timber Prices with Macroeconomic and International Drivers

detail.title: Multi-Horizon Machine Learning Forecasts of Timber Prices with Macroeconomic and International Drivers

declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the National Science Center in Poland (grant no. 2021/43/B/HS4/03371).

detail.abstract:
Timber price forecasting is critical for production planning, contract design, and investment decisions across the construction and pulp and paper industries. The Polish timber market presents a distinctive institutional setting in which the State Forests (Lasy Państwowe) operate as a near-monopoly in timber supply, shaping auction outcomes and market dynamics to an extent unmatched elsewhere in Europe. This system amplifies both local constraints and macro-regional shocks transmitted through trade links with Germany and Finland. Timber prices in Poland are strongly influenced by macroeconomic and policy factors, including inflation, interest rates, energy costs, and EU climate initiatives such as the Fit-for-55 package, as well as by exogenous shocks like the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2022–2023 energy crisis. 

We construct weekly price series (2009–2025) for two major pine assortments — w_standard (sawlogs) and S_S2A (pulpwood) - from e-Drewno auction data and augment them with international timber prices, macro-financial indicators, and housing market variables. A hierarchical feature-selection pipeline combining ridge regression, LightGBM-based importance measures, recursive elimination, and forward selection identifies relevant autoregressive and exogenous predictors with lags of up to 52 weeks. Forecasts are generated using a direct multi-horizon LightGBM approach that trains separate models for each of 26 forecast weeks. Our results show that incorporating macroeconomic and international variables substantially improves medium-term forecast accuracy relative to autoregressive baselines. The importance of explanatory factors differs across assortments, reflecting their distinct industrial uses and sensitivity to economic cycles. The proposed pipeline provides an interpretable, operational framework for rolling updates of timber price forecasts in a quasi-monopolistic market shaped by domestic policy and European climate objectives.

title: The Enforcement of European Digital Regulation: Overlaps and Pathways

detail.title: The Enforcement of European Digital Regulation: Overlaps and Pathways
detail.abstract: The European Union has intensified its regulatory efforts in the digital domain, resulting in a complex and layered legal framework. Significant attention has focused on the lack of coherence across legislation and other regulatory instruments, while less consideration has been given to enforcement, particularly to the expansion of powers and responsibilities distributed across multiple national and supranational authorities. This paper aims to address the primary challenges to the enforcement of the EU digital acquis and explore potential pathways for enhancing its effectiveness. The first part provides examples of how the growing number of EU legal instruments in European digital policy, particularly targeting digital services, has not fully considered the intersections between different technologies and overlapping regulatory frameworks. The second part then underlines how these substantive overlaps translate into enforcement challenges. It addresses the quantitative dimension of the enforcement framework, detailing the multiplicity of bodies involved while analysing the overlapping competences that arise from this institutional complexity from the national and supranational perspectives. The final section explores possible solutions, evaluating opportunities and limitations of various pathways to improve the enforcement of European digital regulation.

detail.abstract: Additive manufacturing of high-performance polymers has emerged as a transformative force in orthopedic device production. Materials such as polyetheretherketone, polyetherketoneketone, and advanced polyamides are increasingly positioned as alternatives to metals in load-bearing applications due to favourable biocompatibility, radiolucency, and tailored mechanical properties. However, despite rapid technological advancement in powder bed fusion and fused filament fabrication systems, significant translational gaps persist between laboratory innovation and commercial-scale adoption. This paper examines the mechanical, regulatory, economic, and innovation-related barriers that limit the widespread commercialization of 3D-printed polymer implants.

title: The Biotech Valuation Puzzle: Why Pipeline Labels Predict Less than Pipeline Activity

detail.title: The Biotech Valuation Puzzle: Why Pipeline Labels Predict Less than Pipeline Activity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of Arcline Research, a biotech decision intelligence platform. The research was conducted independently using publicly available data. No client relationships influenced the analysis or findings.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Standard risk-adjusted net present value frameworks predict that categorical pipeline characteristics — clinical development stage, therapeutic indication, and drug modality — should meaningfully differentiate biotech company valuations. Stage-specific success probabilities, indication-specific market sizes, and modality-specific development costs all enter valuation models as first-order parameters. I test this prediction using 4,117 biotech financing transactions spanning 2008 to 2026, sourced from SEC EDGAR filings and cross-referenced with ClinicalTrials.gov for independent clinical taxonomy assignment. The categorical labels collectively explain less than 5% of pre-money valuation variance beyond deal structure controls. However, continuous measures of the same underlying pipeline construct — the number of active clinical trials, the diversity of development phases represented, and maximum trial enrollment — explain substantially more, outperforming the categorical labels by a factor of 1.4 to 1.6 in partial R². On a matched sample of 1,630 transactions, pipeline activity measures achieve a cross-validated R² of 0.153, compared with 0.115 for the categorical labels. When both are included, the combined model reaches 0.172; activity contributes an incremental 0.057 beyond labels, while labels contribute only 0.019 beyond activity. The asymmetry is the puzzle: the pipeline predicts valuations, but its continuous dimensions carry substantially more information than its categorical classifications. A comprehensive screening of 65 candidate variables contextualizes these findings, revealing that calendar metadata — the day of the week a deal closes — achieves comparable explanatory power to therapeutic indication, a variable with direct theoretical relevance to drug economics. Twenty-five placebo variables confirm the methodology's specificity. These findings suggest that supplementing the comparable transaction framework's categorical filters with continuous pipeline activity measures, available at no cost from public clinical trial registries, could improve valuation precision.

title: From Black Box to Explainable Portfolio Optimization: Tracing Allocations to Views and Constraints
affiliations: BNP Paribas - BNP Paribas Asset Management, BNP Paribas Asset Management, BNP Paribas Asset Management and BNP Paribas Asset Management

detail.title: From Black Box to Explainable Portfolio Optimization: Tracing Allocations to Views and Constraints
detail.abstract: This paper introduces a comprehensive framework to make portfolio optimization fully transparent and explainable in the context of tactical asset allocation. The method breaks down the optimized multi-asset portfolio into a sum of intuitive sub-portfolios, each capturing a distinct driver of the final allocation. Specifically, the decomposition separates the contributions from: (i) a sub-portfolio that replicates the strategic allocation using the available funds, accounting for mismatches between the investable universe and the indices used for the strategic asset allocation; (ii) sub-portfolios with the tilts expressing the tactical allocation views; (iii) a sub-portfolio with tilts arising from expected fund alphas, net of fees; (iv) a set of sub-portfolios quantifying the impact of binding constraints; and (v) a funding sub-portfolio with the adjustment to ensure full investment. We introduce additional practical refinements to enhance the interpretability, robustness, and practical usability of the decomposition. These include a more intuitive normalization of the sub-portfolios and mechanisms for redistributing extreme constraint effects.

title: Stagnant Income and Rising Vulnerability: An Assessment of Agricultural Households in the Period of Doubling Farmers' Income in India
