title: Refugee Resettlement on the Horn of Africa: The Integration of Host and Refugee Land-Use Patterns

detail.title: Refugee Resettlement on the Horn of Africa: The Integration of Host and Refugee Land-Use Patterns
detail.abstract: The enormity of the African refugee problem underscores the importance of resettlement issues in land use planning. Efforts to resettle subsistence-oriented agricultural populations have often come into conflict with host, or in-place land uses as competition for scarce resources lead to land degradation, violence, and the failure of resettlement schemes. The success of refugee resettlement will depend to a large extent on the degree to which host and refugee land-use patterns can become integrated or reconciled. The majority of African refugee populations reside on the Horn and in the Sahel, where arid and semi-arid ecologies predominate and pastoralism is a major form of land-use. This study considers a resettlement design which integrates refugee agricultural land-use patterns with those of the host pastoralist land-use in the context of the frequent droughts which visit the area. Given the magnitude of dislocation problems on the continent, successful resettlement will play an important role in African agriculture and development.

title: Restocking Refugee Pastoralists on the Horn of Africa

detail.title: Restocking Refugee Pastoralists on the Horn of Africa
detail.abstract: Repeated and lingering famine on the Horn of Africa has produced enormous pastoralist refugee populations in a region where livestock production is a major form of land use. Permanently settling destitute pastoralists into pursuits other than herding has a record of failure, can disrupt host land-uses causing social and ecological problems, and can deny utilization of very large grazing areas where pastoralism may be the only ecologically and economically sustainable land-use. Herd reconstitution needs to be considered an option in relief and rehabilitation programs for pastoralists. This paper examines a design where the most proven and immediate way of sustaining stockless pastoralists-farming-can be used to facilitate restocking objectives. With data gathered in Somalia, estimates of livestock carrying capacity are linked with: characteristics of forage resources, land area, livestock units, and frequency of good, average, and poor (drought) water years, in order to explore the possibilities for incorporating restocking into refugee rehabilitation efforts.

title: Management of Spatially Extensive Natural Resources in Postwar Contexts: Working with the Peace Process

detail.title: Management of Spatially Extensive Natural Resources in Postwar Contexts: Working with the Peace Process
detail.abstract: While extensively occurring natural resources play a fundamental role in the survival and recovery of postwar populations, their management is not presently part of the operational priorities in a peace process. Dependence on naturally occurring food, fuel, water, secure locations, and products that can be obtained and sold quickly for dislocated, war-weary populations is a primary approach to postwar livelihoods. The peace process however focuses on the logistical and institutional aspects of security, demobilization, reintegration and humanitarian efforts. The result is profound degradation of the spatially extensive resources necessary for longer-term recovery. The primary reason for the inattention to resource degradation in a peace process is that conventional conservation approaches do not fit with the priorities of a peace process or attend to the immediate needs of a postwar population; designed as they are for stable, peaceful settings. This article focuses on the need to derive postwar natural resource management approaches which can work with the in-place priorities of a peace process. Four such approaches are suggested, with successful examples from specific countries.

title: An Examined Education
affiliations: School of Social and Political Sciences, University of Lincoln

detail.title: An Examined Education
detail.abstract: What is the value of tests in education? Encouraging learning and establishing merit are traditional justifications for stressful ordeals such as competitive examinations. Some critics argue that these approaches negatively impact students' well-being and do not represent essential experiences for future life and work. As a result, higher education in the United Kingdom has seen less attention on proven knowledge acquisition and formal testing in favour of alternative modes of coursework assessment perceived to be less stressful and, therefore, more accessible. Drawing on Adam Smith's moral psychology from The Theory of Moral Sentiments, this article argues that this understandable drive to reduce unpleasant experiences associated with learning denies students important opportunities to mature as well as the pleasure associated with clearly demonstrating one's educational achievement.

title: Reclaiming Finance: Taming Capital and Human Nature Through the "Institutional Cage"-A Theoretical Analysis from the Perspective of Human Nature Institutionalism
affiliations: and Soochow University

detail.title: Reclaiming Finance: Taming Capital and Human Nature Through the "Institutional Cage"-A Theoretical Analysis from the Perspective of Human Nature Institutionalism
detail.abstract: In response to Professor Wang Defeng's controversial assertion that "finance is an evil discipline", this paper adopts China's indigenous original theory of Human Nature Institutionalism as the analytical framework to systematically deconstruct the neutral essence and alienation logic of financial instruments, and deepen the core consensus that "tools are neither good nor evil; morality lies in humans and institutions". Human Nature Institutionalism takes "short-sightedness, self-interest and risk aversion" as its core axiom, integrates behavioral economics, institutional economics and evolutionary psychology, and constructs a complete theoretical system of "axiom-theorem-tool". The study finds that the essence of financial alienation lies in the malicious inducement of human nature by financial institutions through the "benefit perception function" in the absence of institutional constraints; the key to breaking the dilemma is to build a collaborative governance system featuring "macrolevel anti-empty-promising, meso-level damping optimization, micro-level combination of rigidity and flexibility, and statutory human nature review". Through in-depth deconstruction of Collateralized Debt Obligation (CDO) products and case analysis of the "Five-Pillar Supervision" system implemented by the National Financial Regulatory Administration, this paper verifies the explanatory power and practicality of the theory. Furthermore, aiming at the problem of algorithmic short-sightedness in the era of financial technology, it proposes the "algorithmic damping" mechanism and AI-assisted regulatory solutions. The core contribution of this study is to deeply integrate indigenous original theory with financial governance practices, provide an operable institutional framework for finance to "promote good and curb evil", and offer a non-Western-centric Chinese solution for global financial governance.

title: The Impact of Flood Risk on England's Property Market
affiliations: and City University London - The Business School

detail.title: The Impact of Flood Risk on England's Property Market
detail.abstract:
• Based on our sample, one out of six properties in England are at risk of flooding and around half of those affected properties can be characterised as high risk. This is in line with current insurance underwriting assessments. 

• Findings show that residential properties in England with flood risk are sold at a 8.14% discount compared to non-affected properties. The level of the price discount is strongly correlated with the probability of flood risk. The price discount reaches 31.3% for very high risk properties. 

• The average flood risk of sold properties in the England between 2006 and 2021 is estimated at 8.01 per cent, compared to unsold property flood risk of 8.63 per cent. Zero exposure to flooding increases the saleability of a property from 63.3 per cent to 65.6 per cent, however flood risk is never the main driver of a sale. 

• The regions most exposed to flood risk are East Anglia, North West and Yorkshire, where around 13%-18% of properties are affected. In terms of property types, semi-detached and terraced houses are more vulnerable to flooding since any temporary protection measures, such as blocking doors, windows, vents and pipes, will not be effective unless their neighbours take similar steps. 

• Between 2050 and 2080, property-level flood risk is projected to increase further by 8%. Our empirical model suggests that one percentage point increase in properties’ flood risk is associated with a decline of 0.11-0.19% in both sold and asking price. 

• Our results suggest that market participants tend to underestimate the probability of flooding. Therefore, after periods of extreme weather events the one percentage point increase in flood risk results in a greater price discount (0.17 - 0.20%) for a short period. 

• The research also confirms that the effect of flood risk is asymmetric and buyers of lower-priced properties are more sensitive towards flood risk compared to buyers of more expensive properties. A one percentage point increase in flood risk is associated with 0.16% discount in properties priced within the lower quantile of the sample, 0.13% for properties priced around the sample median and 0.10% for properties priced within the upper quantile of the sample.

title: Finite-Sample Long-Memory Estimation via Detectability Boundaries
affiliations: Fordham University

detail.title: Finite-Sample Long-Memory Estimation via Detectability Boundaries
detail.abstract: We propose a finite-sample framework for removing long-range dependence in equity log-price series based on a detectability boundary dLTM: the largest fractional differencing order at which hyperbolic ACF tail structure remains statistically distinguishable from noise. Under stationary ARFIMA dynamics, dLTM satisfies dLTM ≈ d* −d0, where d* is the true fractional integration order and d0 is a finite-sample resolution limit. Monte Carlo calibration yields the scaling law for ARFIMA ^d0(T) = 5.81·T−0.367 (R2 = 0.999), with d0 = 0.30 at T = 3,200 and d0 = 0.20 at T =10,000. In market data, regime heterogeneity and volatility clustering make d0 persistence estimator instead of true memory, making dLTM a reliable differencing index in practice. Applied to the S&P 500 universe over 2010–2020, dLTM is estimated on a rolling n = 2,400 window and evaluated monthly against a fixed d = 0.5 benchmark across 484 assets. dLTM produces whiter AR(1) residuals in 70–90% of assets at every evaluation date over a full decade. The win rate rises monotonically from near 50% when dLTM ≈ 0.5 to 97–100% in the quartile where the two approaches diverge most, and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test rejects equality at p <0.0001 at every date. Results hold broadly across sectors.

title: Wage Flexibility, Trend Inflation, and Welfare in a Currency Union
affiliations: University of Melbourne and University of Southampton

detail.title: Wage Flexibility, Trend Inflation, and Welfare in a Currency Union
detail.abstract: This paper revisits the welfare consequences of wage flexibility in a currency union model in which member countries face limited monetary autonomy. Earlier studies conclude that, under a zero inflation target, greater wage flexibility can be welfare-reducing because it increases the volatility of price and wage inflation. However, we show that this result reverses when the inflation target is positive. We find that trend inflation affects the welfare consequences of wage flexibility primarily through changes in the constant term capturing the steady-state utility cost arising from price and wage dispersion, rather than through changes in volatilities. Greater wage flexibility reduces this steady-state cost, which dominates the increased welfare losses associated with higher price and wage inflation volatility. This result holds in both a simple analytical model and a medium-scale model with realistic features.

title: Harvest FIRE: Increasing Lifetime Consumption by 25-60% Without Increasing Ruin Risk

detail.title: Harvest FIRE: Increasing Lifetime Consumption by 25-60% Without Increasing Ruin Risk

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available financial market data and does not involve human subjects. Ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Conventional retirement withdrawal research has focused on minimizing portfolio ruin probability, treating survival as the primary success criterion. However, a portfolio that survives 30 years with substantial residual wealth implies systematic underspendingconsumption capacity that was generated but never utilized. This paper introduces Harvest FIRE, a dynamic withdrawal framework that redefines retirement optimization as a constrained consumption-maximization problem. The framework operates on a predominantly equity portfolio with a cash buffer and incorporates three mechanisms: (1) a guaranteed base withdrawal of 4% of initial wealth, inflation-adjusted, which serves as a consumption floor rather than a ceiling; (2) a performance-based bonus that transfers surplus above a linear depletion path into consumption, at reward ratios of 15-30%; and (3) a user-defined depletion slope that converts terminal wealth from an uncontrolled residual into a design variable. An optional Seeding mechanism redeploys cash reserves into equities following large drawdowns, exploiting the statistical tendency for above-average returns after market declines. While equity concentration increases short-term portfolio volatility, the framework absorbs this through consumption flexibility and the cash buffer rather than asset-allocation shifts. Using 20,000 Monte Carlo simulations and 47 rolling 30-year historical back-tests of S&P 500 total-return data (1950-2024), we compare five strategies: the traditional 4% rule (60/40), a three-layer bucket strategy, and three Harvest variants (15%, 30%, and 30% with Seeding). Harvest strategies increase median lifetime consumption by 22-53% in Monte Carlo simulations and by 24-64% in historical backtests, while maintaining comparable success rates. Terminal-wealth variance is markedly reduced under all Harvest variants, indicating more efficient conversion of assets into lifetime consumption. Our findings suggest that exclusive reliance on ruin minimization may overlook an equally important dimension of retirement risk: systematic underspending.

title: WTO's Dispute Settlement, MPIA, and India
affiliations: Jindal Global Law School, O P Jindal Global University  and University of Sussex

detail.title: WTO's Dispute Settlement, MPIA, and India

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of World Trade, Volume 60, Issue 3/4 (forthcoming)

detail.abstract: The establishment of a two-tier dispute settlement system at the WTO has significantly judicialized international trade relations. However, this process is currently hindered by the Appellate Body's dysfunction. In the absence of the Appellate Body, the Multi-Party Interim Arbitration (MPIA) Arrangement is partially bridging the gap. This MPIA initiative aims to restore the WTO's two-tier dispute settlement system and has recently gained traction, garnering support from 57 countries. However, India, a crucial developing-country member, has not joined the MPIA, despite its ongoing call for the restoration of the Appellate Body. Most of India's concerns regarding the MPIA do not hold up under scrutiny. Contrary to India's argument, joining the MPIA would not diminish its position in advocating for the restoration of the Appellate Body. Furthermore, although the United States-India's key trading partneris not a member of the MPIA, India can still invoke the MPIA in disputes with other significant players, such as the European Union and Japan. As the multilateral trading system faces increasing challenges, countries like India need to build alliances and develop innovative solutions. Supporting the MPIA is one such step toward restoring the WTO's judicial function and should be embraced by India.

title: The Collapse of the Shrimp Industry in Mozambique’s Coastal Triggered by the White Spot Syndrome Virus (WSSV): A Qualitative Case Study
affiliations: Universidade Eduardo Mondlane, Faculty of Arts and Social Sciences, UEM, Universidade Eduardo Mondlane, Eduardo Mondlane University (UEM), Eduardo Mondlane University (UEM), Eduardo Mondlane University (UEM), Universidade Eduardo Mondlane, Universidade Eduardo Mondlane and Norwegian University of Life Sciences

detail.title: The Collapse of the Shrimp Industry in Mozambique’s Coastal Triggered by the White Spot Syndrome Virus (WSSV): A Qualitative Case Study
detail.abstract:
Mozambique is one of the countries with the greatest potential for shrimp production, due to its species diversity, favourable climate, and abundant water bodies. Despite this potential, the shrimp industry remained underdeveloped. However, to date, only White Spot Syndrome Virus has been considered the only factor affecting the shrimp industry. This study examines how other factors including technological, environmental, economic, political-institutional, and socio-cultural, contributed to the development and collapse of the shrimp industry. 
Specifically, the aim was to identify and analyse the factors that influenced the dynamics of the shrimp aquaculture industry.,The approach used was qualitative, semi-structured interviews conducted with 30 participants divided into three target groups: researchers, representatives of government aquaculture agencies, and workers in aquaculture companies in seven coastal provinces. The data was analysed using thematic analysis.,
The results show that the presence of WSSV in the environment is an important factor for shrimp industry; however, there are other critical structural factors affecting underdevelopment of shrimp industry, including lack of the introduction of technologies such as Biofloc systems and the use of pathogen-free postlarvae (SPF), high cost of imported feed, lack of capital, dissatisfaction among workers, lack of government support, and local cultural beliefs.,
It is concluded that the problems facing Mozambique's shrimp aquaculture are not just disease control, but stem from more interdependent structural flaws. The circumstances need a shift in industrial management, with an emphasis on implementing suitable technologies, facilitating funding and input access, and honouring regional cultural values.

title: The Ordo-Causal Attribution Deficit: A Prudential Capital Framework for Autonomous Multi-Agent Coding Systems in Financial Infrastructure

detail.title: The Ordo-Causal Attribution Deficit: A Prudential Capital Framework for Autonomous Multi-Agent Coding Systems in Financial Infrastructure
detail.abstract: The proliferation of agentic coding systems-software that writes software-has precipitated a structural lacuna in financial supervision. This Ordo-Causal Attribution Deficit describes the inability of existing prudential frameworks to assign legal duty, supervisory jurisdiction, and liability in chains of automated code generation that extend across days, multiple agentic nodes, and organizational boundaries. As the 2026 Agentic Coding Trends Report demonstrates, financial institutions now deploy "long-running agents" capable of building complete systems over extended periods with "minimal human intervention," while multi-agent orchestration creates emergent behaviours that defy linear causation. Current regulatory architectures assume proximate human oversight and discrete, attributable acts of programming. When autonomous agents generate code that modifies core banking systems, creates financial algorithms, or deploys customer-facing interfaces, the traditional nexus between human intent, supervisory duty, and prudential outcome fractures. This framework addresses the deficit by establishing forensic standards for agentic causation, a quantifiable risk assessment protocol, and capital-based incentives that internalize the externalities of unsupervised machine generation in financial services.

title: Do Stock Buybacks Cause Harm? Evidence from Financially Distressed Firms
affiliations: , INSEAD - Finance and University of Colorado Boulder

detail.title: Do Stock Buybacks Cause Harm? Evidence from Financially Distressed Firms

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None of the authors have a conflict of interest to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: n/a

detail.abstract: Critics argue that buybacks weaken firms and harm stakeholders. This has prompted U.S. policymakers to repeatedly consider restricting or even banning them despite a rich literature generally favorable to buybacks. This literature, though, is weak with respect to assessing harm as it generally focuses on shareholder outcomes among healthy firms and thus cannot address the broader concerns regulators harbor. We examine firms near financial distress where the adverse effects of a buyback should be most evident. Contrary to critics' claims, there is no evidence of underinvestment, excessive leverage, reduced innovation, diminished production, bankruptcy or adverse employment effects. We find no basis for regulatory intervention.

title: Preface to The Public Pension Crisis: Contractual Rights and Constitutional Limits
affiliations: Robert H. Smith School of Business

detail.title: Preface to The Public Pension Crisis: Contractual Rights and Constitutional Limits
detail.abstract: Public sector pensions face persistent demographic upheaval and financial fragility amid a turbulent political context. With limited choices in how to shore up failing pension plans, state and local governments have been enacting legislation to trim pension benefits. Current and former government employees have challenged such reforms in state and federal courts across the United States. My motivation in writing this book was to furnish a timely analytical lens for comprehending these contemporary constitutional controversies. A central puzzle in the emerging jurisprudence about government pensions is the protection afforded by contract law under state and U.S. Contract Clauses as well as state Pension Clauses. This is the first book to analyze the extent that pension benefits are contractual obligations. Questions about whether and when pensions are contracts have been surprisingly difficult to explain. While the answers have important practical implications, the line between contract and no contract remains elusive. It is this pressing jurisprudential problem that this book seeks to solve.

title: Network-Augmented Volatility Forecasting with Idiosyncratic Jump Spillovers
affiliations: University of Oxford - Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance,  and University of Oxford - Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance

detail.title: Network-Augmented Volatility Forecasting with Idiosyncratic Jump Spillovers
detail.abstract: Empirical studies often conclude that jump variation contributes little to realized volatility (RV) forecasting in univariate settings. We revisit this question from a crosssectional perspective, asking whether jump shocks propagate across stocks through network channels and improve RV forecasts. Using high-frequency data for S&P 100 stocks over 2007-2021, we construct idiosyncratic returns via factor regressions and estimate sparse dependency networks from these residuals. Combining these networks with HAR-type predictors in linear (GHAR-JV) and graph neural network (GNNHAR-JV) models, we find that idiosyncratic-network-based specifications reduce one-dayahead MSE by around 30% relative to a standard HAR benchmark, while jump models on raw or market-based networks deliver little benefit. We conclude that jump variation becomes economically important once viewed as an idiosyncratic network spillover mechanism, and that structured network learning enhances volatility forecasting performance, while preserving an economically interpretable cross-sectional structure.

title: When the Treasury Does Monetary Policy
affiliations: , Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy and Northwestern University

detail.title: When the Treasury Does Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: Debt management decisions have macroeconomic effects comparable to monetary policy. Using high-frequency movements in interest rate futures around U.S. Treasury issuance announcements, we identify a Treasury policy shock-an unanticipated change in public debt supply across maturities. A shock that raises the five-year Treasury yield transmits strongly to corporate borrowing rates, tightens credit conditions, and lowers industrial production significantly. These effects closely mirror those of a conventional monetary policy tightening. While long-term Treasury yields increase significantly, the shock has minimal effects on short-term interest rates. We show that this pattern reflects the Federal Reserve's sterilization of short-term Treasury issuance, while issuance at longer maturities is only partially offset.

title: Reaching for Yield in Turbulent Times: Bank Liquidity Creation under Geopolitical Risk
affiliations: , Fordham University  , The University of Sydney - Discipline of Finance and The University of Sydney - Discipline of Finance

detail.title: Reaching for Yield in Turbulent Times: Bank Liquidity Creation under Geopolitical Risk
detail.abstract: Using a panel of commercial banks from 40 countries between 2001 and 2023, we find that heightened geopolitical risk (GPR) markedly increases bank liquidity creation. Exploiting the 2022 Russia-Ukraine war as a quasi-natural experiment, we identify this effect through a difference-indifferences framework that leverages both geographic exposure and trade linkages with the conflict region. The increase in liquidity creation is primarily profit-driven: banks expand lending, reduce cash holdings, and earn higher interest margins and returns during periods of elevated geopolitical tension. We find little evidence for alternative explanations, such as government intervention, precautionary borrowing, or monetary easing. The effect is more pronounced among larger, more profitable banks in competitive banking systems, but weakens during banking crises. Our findings highlight the strategic supply-side role of banks in responding to geopolitical risk, positioning GPR as a key external driver of financial intermediation.

title: Do ESG Scores Decouple Energy Stocks from Commodities? Evidence from the U.S. Energy Market
affiliations: , University of Aberdeen and University of Aberdeen

detail.title: Do ESG Scores Decouple Energy Stocks from Commodities? Evidence from the U.S. Energy Market
detail.abstract: Despite the crucial influence of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors on energy markets, its role in driving the nexus between energy stocks and commodities is yet to be explored. Employing a TVP-VAR model, this study investigates the impact of ESG scores on the Pairwise Connectedness Indices (PCIs) between stocks of U.S. oil and gas firms and key fossil energy commodities. Overall, we find that the return connectedness indices are significant and time-varying across energy assets within each network. Additionally, the Pairwise Connectedness Indices (PCIs) indicate strong bilateral transmission effects between energy stocks and fossil fuel markets during the sample period. The fixed effects panel regression results reveal that ESG scores weaken the pairwise connections between energy stocks and commodities, thereby reinforcing the stability channel relative to the transition channel. However, findings are heterogeneous across the three pillars and at different quantiles. The results also suggest that the Global Financial Crisis and the European Debt Crisis intensify ESG’s influence, whereas COVID-19 moderates its effect.

title: The Shape of Beta: Industry Factor Structure and Crisis Risk Premium
affiliations: Amazon Web Services Inc and Korea University

detail.title: The Shape of Beta: Industry Factor Structure and Crisis Risk Premium
detail.abstract: We document that stocks within the same industry share a common factor exposure structure—an "industry beta shape"—and that deviations from this shape predict future returns during financial crises. Using CRSP data covering 4,240 U.S. stocks across 46 industries from 2004 to 2024, we estimate firm-level Fama-French five-factor betas and characterize the cross-sectional structure of beta matrices within each industry. We find that the top two singular values of the industry beta matrix explain 82% of its variance, indicating substantial commonality in factor exposures. Exploiting this structure through cross-sectional shrinkage improves out-of-sample return prediction by 7.5% relative to OLS, with positive improvement in all 36 industries tested. Stocks whose factor exposures deviate from the industry norm earna crisis risk premium: the quintile spread is economically large during the Global Financial Crisis (+19.0%/year) and COVID-19 (+27.3%/year) but negligible in tranquil periods. This spread survives controls for firm size, is concentrated in large-capitalization stocks (t = 4.42), and is robust to transaction costs. The signal requires a rich factor model (FF5 > FF3 > CAPM), suggesting that multi-dimensional factor exposure heterogeneity, rather than simple market beta dispersion, drives the premium.

title: Moving the Goalposts: The Changing Objectives of Industrial Policy
affiliations: European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) - Office of the Chief Economist

detail.title: Moving the Goalposts: The Changing Objectives of Industrial Policy

publicationDetails.journalName: European Bank for Reconstruction & Development Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper relies on a novel dataset of more than 31,000 industrial policies in 150 economies over the period 2009-2022 to codify and examine the stated objectives of these policies and their characteristics. We find that industrial policies increasingly pursue multiple objectives, often ones that may be hard to reconcile. In a two-way fixed effects framework, we show that industrial policies with environmental objectives are more common in Western economies while secure supply objectives are more common in economies geopolitically aligned with China. The majority of industrial policies have features that may make them "addictive": they discriminate against foreigners, are firm-specific and lack "sunset clauses". Such addictive policies are more common in economies in rival geopolitical blocs and those with better administrative capacity, suggesting that political economy tends to dominate government effectiveness when it comes to the design of industrial policies.

title: Mapping the Local Youth Violence Prevention Ecosystem: A Foundational Study for Diversion and Navigator Mentorship Pathways
affiliations: Oxford Brookes University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Mapping the Local Youth Violence Prevention Ecosystem: A Foundational Study for Diversion and Navigator Mentorship Pathways
detail.abstract: Background Violence is a major public health issue, disproportionately affecting children and young people and contributing to educational disengagement and later harm. Within serious violence prevention policy in England, emerging evidence highlights the promise of mentorship-based Navigator models in engaging vulnerable youth. Focused Diversion extends this approach upstream, targeting earlier vulnerability; however, sustained outcomes depend on effective transition into community provision, positioning referral connectivity as a critical protective mechanism within local violence reduction systems. To address this gap, the study develops and applies a novel prevention systems-mapping framework. Method A structured service-mapping and documentary analysis was undertaken, informed by public health and realist perspectives, to assess community prevention infrastructure, referral connectivity, and evidence alignment within violence reduction ecosystems. Publicly available service directories and organisational sources were systematically reviewed to identify sustained, community-based provision for children and young people across five (redacted) areas. Services were classified by delivery characteristics and aligned to Youth Endowment Fund Toolkit categories to assess evidence strength. Findings Mapping identified a prevention landscape dominated by universal, activity-led provision, particularly sports and after-school programmes, forming the primary engagement infrastructure. Targeted and specialist interventions were present but limited. Provision was largely open-access and delivered through community-anchored, place-based settings. Evidence alignment showed concentration in mid-evidence, variable-impact models, with notable opportunity for developing transition and seasonal provision. Discussion/Conclusion The mapping highlights a prevention system with a strong universal foundation but opportunities to strengthen depth, connectivity, and continuity. Thinner targeted and specialist layers may constrain progression for higher-need cohorts exposed to escalating violence risk. Transition and seasonal gaps, particularly summer employment, represent missed prevention opportunities during periods of heightened vulnerability. The framework demonstrates utility as both an analytical and operational tool, informing step-down pathways, commissioning, and the embedding of community provision within a public health violence prevention approach.

title: Photons = Tokens: The Physics of AI and the Economics of Knowledge
affiliations: , University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and George Mason University

detail.title: Photons = Tokens: The Physics of AI and the Economics of Knowledge
detail.abstract: Debates about artificial intelligence capabilities and risks are often conducted without quantitative grounding. This paper applies the methodology of MacKay [2009]who reframed energy policy as arithmetic-to the economy of AI computation. We define the token, the elementary unit of large language model input and output, as a physical quantity with measurable thermodynamic cost. Using Landauer's principle, Shannon's channel capacity, and current infrastructure data, we construct a supply-and-demand balance sheet for global token production. We then derive a finite question budget: the number of meaningful queries humanity can direct at AI systems under physical, information-theoretic, and economic constraints. We apply Coase's theory of the firm and the durable-goods monopoly problem to the AI value chain-from photon to atom to chip to power to token to question-to identify where economic value concentrates and where regulatory intervention is warranted. We argue that the expansion of the token budget does not resolve a deeper constraint: under structural uncertainty, the decisive variable is not how many questions can be answered but which questions are worth asking-a problem of agency and direction that computation alone cannot solve. We connect limits of measurement in the token economy to a structural parallel between Goodhart's law and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, and to Arrow's impossibility result for efficient information pricing. The framework yields order-of-magnitude estimates that discipline policy discussion: at current efficiency, the projected 2028 US AI energy allocation of 326 TWh could support roughly 6.5 × 10 17 tokens per year, or 225,000 tokens per person per day-more than three orders of magnitude above estimated mid-2024 utilization.

reference: Texas A&M University School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper
title: How Tech Took Over
affiliations: Texas A&M University School of Law

detail.title: How Tech Took Over

publicationDetails.detailsText: Texas A&M University School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Texas A&M University School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Technology firms play key roles in public governance. Their products enable forms of reasoning and data processing that modern agencies must use. Their data permits modes of analysis and surveillance that are crucial to governing populations yet, without private cooperation, would be out of reach. By now, critiques of the power of Silicon Valley could fill Alexandria: opaque, unaccountable, biased, ineffective, corrupt, self-serving, monopolistic, manipulative, anti-democratic. And yet, much like the telegraph, the railroad, and the automobile, cloud computing and artificial intelligence are rapidly remaking markets, social relations, and the state itself.

Tech’s entrenchment in public governance requires both a new understanding of how tech companies became so powerful and a new account of the constitutional implications of this transformation. Tech companies did not become integral to public governance by accident, nor did they ascend simply because—as many critics have pointed out—the federal government failed to regulate Silicon Valley during and after the 1990s. Instead, decades of legal and policy interventions forged an enduring, expanding role for technology companies in statecraft. Today, the tech industry plays a central role in securing American geopolitical dominance, supporting government infrastructure, and facilitating flows of data.

Understanding both what technology companies do to govern and how they came to occupy such an important role in the state permits a new perspective on the constitutional costs of this arrangement. In their current role, tech companies are integral to public governance, but they neither represent nor are accountable to the public. At stake is not merely whether the existing distribution of power is consistent with constitutional doctrine or the text. Instead, recognizing tech companies’ exercise of public power also means reckoning with the permanent transformations to governance that they have wrought.

title: Tax reporting under GRI 207: an exploratory case study of Shell plc
affiliations: Griffith University, Griffith Business School, Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics, Students, Curtin University - Curtin Law School, Griffith University, Griffith Business School, Department of Accounting, Finance and Economics, Students and Griffith University

detail.title: Tax reporting under GRI 207: an exploratory case study of Shell plc
detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of the Global Reporting Initiative's GRI 207: Tax 2019 standard on corporate tax transparency and tax behaviour, using Shell plc as a longitudinal case study from 2011 to 2023. It critically evaluates how GRI 207 interacts with the UK's existing disclosure frameworks, assesses whether it introduces new dimensions of transparency, and examines its influence on Shell's tax disclosure and tax aggressiveness. The study finds that GRI 207 largely complements the UK's existing tax disclosure requirements, particularly in strategy, governance, and stakeholder engagement, but diverges by advocating public country-by-country reporting, which Shell has not fully adopted. Further, tax disclosure volume increased significantly following the introduction of GRI 207; however, effective tax rates (ETRs) and adjusted ETRs declined, suggesting increased tax aggressiveness. The study concludes that GRI 207, as a voluntary and soft-law initiative, enhances public reporting, but its impact on corporate tax behaviour, particularly in Shell's case, appears limited.

title: A Bipartite Graph Approach to U.S.-China Cross-Market Return Forecasting
affiliations: University of Oxford - Department of Statistics, Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Erasmus School of Economics, University of Oxford - Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance and

detail.title: A Bipartite Graph Approach to U.S.-China Cross-Market Return Forecasting
detail.abstract: This paper studies cross-market return predictability through a machine learning framework that preserves economic structure. Exploiting the non-overlapping trading hours of the U.S. and Chinese equity markets, we construct a directed bipartite graph that captures time-ordered predictive linkages between stocks across markets. Edges are selected via rolling-window hypothesis testing, and the resulting graph serves as a sparse, economically interpretable feature-selection layer for downstream machine learning models. We apply a range of regularized and ensemble methods to forecast open-to-close returns using lagged foreign-market information. Our results reveal a pronounced directional asymmetry: U.S. previous-close-to-close returns contain substantial predictive information for Chinese intraday returns, whereas the reverse effect is limited. This informational asymmetry translates into economically meaningful performance differences and highlights how structured machine learning frameworks can uncover cross-market dependencies while maintaining interpretability.

title: Electrifying Mobility Reshapes Cities, Energy Demand, and Emissions in Emerging Economies
affiliations: Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU) - ifo Institute (Leibniz Institute for Economic Research at the University of Munich), Mercator Research Institute on Global Commons and Climate Change (MCC) and Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU)

detail.title: Electrifying Mobility Reshapes Cities, Energy Demand, and Emissions in Emerging Economies
detail.abstract: EV adoption in emerging economies (lower-middle income, fast urbanization and income growth) mitigates emissions of greenhouse gases and local pollutants from gasoline consumption, but at the same time exacerbates urban sprawl. This implies longer driving distances for commuting and non-work trips and higher consumption of floor space per capita and related energy demand for cooling/heating. We model scenarios of full electrification of transport in China, India, Brazil, and Nigeria until 2060, accounting for income growth, population growth, urbanization, public-transport shares, and power-mix scenarios for each country. On average in 2040, 209 percent of the direct carbon emission savings from EV adoption are offset by additional sprawl through increasing VKT (22 percent) and growing energy demand in the building sector (187 percent). Additional urban sprawl from EV adoption leads to the development of 1.2 million square kilometers until 2060. This is equivalent to 32 percent of arable land in 2024.

title: Silencing Pollution: The Environmental Consequences of Anti-SLAPP Laws
affiliations: California State University, Fresno - Craig School of Business, The University of Technology Sydney and University of Melbourne

detail.title: Silencing Pollution: The Environmental Consequences of Anti-SLAPP Laws

keywords.keywords: Anti-SLAPP Statutes; Freedom of Speech; Corporate Environmental Performance; Environmental Investment; Environmental Governance

detail.abstract: We examine whether free-speech protections influence corporate environmental performance. Using the staggered enactment of U.S. anti-SLAPP statutes in a stacked difference-indifferences design from 1990 to 2019, we find that these laws significantly reduce firms' toxic emissions without curbing economic activity. Anti-SLAPP enactments also promote environmental investment, through green innovation, abatement spending, and waste reduction management, and strengthen governance via improved sustainability oversight, ESG-linked executive pay, employee training, and supply chain management. The effects are stronger when stakeholder monitoring is stronger and when managerial incentives embed sustainability goals. Overall, free-speech protections generate powerful environmental benefits.

title: OpenClaw and the Anatomy of Contemporary AI Hype: A Methodological Audit and the Case for Large Understanding Models (LUM)

detail.title: OpenClaw and the Anatomy of Contemporary AI Hype: A Methodological Audit and the Case for Large Understanding Models (LUM)
detail.abstract:
This article provides a structured audit of OpenClaw’s methodological novelty and the socio-epistemic dynamics that converted a tooling-and-orchestration project into a widely perceived “paradigm shift.” Using primary sources (official blog posts, documentation, and repository metadata), peer-reviewed literature on LLMs, tool-using agents, and causality, and a qualitative compilation of media and social metrics, we compare OpenClaw’s architecture to (i) baseline LLM capabilities and (ii) a proposed Large Understanding Model (LUM) paradigm. We find that OpenClaw’s innovations are predominantly systems engineering (channel integration, agent runtime, configuration surfaces, tool/skill packaging, and operational scaffolding) rather than model-level innovations (new learning objectives, grounded semantics, or causal reasoning guarantees).

We then show how hype followed recognizable mechanisms—informational cascades, availability-driven judgment, authority bias, and incentive alignment—while simultaneously exposing unresolved security and governance challenges inherent in agentic systems. We conclude with a concrete experimental validation agenda to separate “agentic productivity” from “understanding,” and discuss research and policy implications for evaluating and deploying autonomous agent infrastructures.

title: Norms in Conflict: Why AI Advisors Fail to Improve Human Coordination
affiliations: , George Mason University, University of Bath and Purdue University - Krannert School of Management

detail.title: Norms in Conflict: Why AI Advisors Fail to Improve Human Coordination
detail.abstract: Cooperation failures in social dilemmas persist because individually rational behavior yields inefficient collective outcomes. Advances in AI raise two possibilities: AI may improve outcomes by advising humans or by acting autonomously. We test both in a repeated threshold public-goods experiment with heterogeneous valuations of the public good. Such threshold games model a broad class of burden-sharing problems (crowdfunding, shared infrastructure, multilateral agreements) in which efficiency requires not only coordination but agreement on a cost-sharing norm. We compare a human-only benchmark to treatments with an AI advisor (OpenAI's GPT-5) and to treatments in which AI agents make allocations directly. AI Only groups outperform human groups, reaching the threshold more often. The mechanism is illuminating: AI agents contribute near-equal amounts largely independent of valuations, whereas humans scale contributions with valuations. In contrast, AI advisors do not improve human-only outcomes. We distinguish two bottlenecks to coordination-an information bottleneck, in which parties lack the calculations needed to condition on others' behavior, and a legitimacy bottleneck, in which parties reject cost-sharing rules that conflict with their fairness norms. AI overcomes the first but not the second.

title: Sparse Portfolios and Benchmarking in Corporate Bond Markets
affiliations: , London Business School and

detail.title: Sparse Portfolios and Benchmarking in Corporate Bond Markets

declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by the Fama-Miller Center for Research in Finance at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business.

detail.abstract: We use detailed data on fixed-income benchmark indexes in Canada and the United States to provide systematic evidence of how benchmarking shapes corporate bond ownership and prices. Funds hold sparse portfolios, and index weights strongly influence which bonds active and passive funds select. We rationalize these patterns in a model with benchmarked managers who face portfolio management costs, which predicts which assets managers optimally include in their portfolios. In the model, a bond's price increases with its benchmarking intensity (BMI)–a measure of the amount of fund capital benchmarked against the bond–while portfolio sparsity attenuates this price impact for excluded bonds. Exploiting discontinuities in benchmarked assets around bond maturity cutoffs, we show that increases in bonds' BMIs lead to reductions in yield spreads and increases in fund ownership–but only for bonds predicted to enter sparse portfolios.

title: Growth, Firm Scale, and the Energy Intensity of Production
affiliations: Columbia University, Columbia University and Columbia University

detail.title: Growth, Firm Scale, and the Energy Intensity of Production
detail.abstract: We uncover a new mechanism that links growth and a decline in the energy intensity of production, observed globally since 1990. Using microdata from India and a causal research design, we demonstrate that the expenditure share of energy declines steeply with firm scale, due both to physical scaling laws and technology investment. Given the fact that average firm size increases with growth, this scale dependence in energy demand implies that production endogenously becomes less energy-intensive with aggregate growth. We develop a model of this mechanism in general equilibrium, and quantify significant reductions in aggregate energy intensity as low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) like India grow. We conclude with a discussion of the future path of emissions in India.

title: The Geopolitics of Food and Agriculture
affiliations: ,  and University of Minnesota - Twin Cities - Department of Applied Economics

detail.title: The Geopolitics of Food and Agriculture
detail.abstract: Food has long served as an instrument of statecraft. Yet agricultural economics typically analyzes policy through the lens of consumer and producer welfare, which neglects security externalities. We review the literature at the intersection of agricultural economics and political science, examining how food systems both shape and are shaped by geopolitical forces through the two channels of (i) domestic instability with international spillovers, and (ii) the deliberate use of food in statecraft. Our synthesis of key findings in the literature suggests that (i) food prices relate to riots and instability while ambiguously relating to civil war and violence, (ii) the wide geographic spread of agriculture limits but does not eliminate unilateral coercive leverage compared with other strategic sectors, and (iii) domestic food policies are strongly related to national security goals. Moreover, we point out the many extant data sets one can use to do work in this area and identify several research gaps in the literature. As global uncertainty intensifies, integrating geopolitical analysis into agricultural economics is essential for policy relevance.

title: Exploring the Career Development of Young People With Refugee Backgrounds: Finding Voice Through Narrative Inquiry
affiliations: Griffith University - School of Psychology

detail.title: Exploring the Career Development of Young People With Refugee Backgrounds: Finding Voice Through Narrative Inquiry
detail.abstract:
The number of forcibly displaced people in recent years has been the greatest since comprehensive statistics on global forced displacement have been collected. As of 2017, approximately 66 million people were forcibly displaced. Of these, nearly 1.2 million, primarily children and young people are estimated to be in urgent need of resettlement in other countries. However, the office of the United Nations’ High Commissioner for Refugees’ Resettlement Program is the only available resettlement program and the limited number of countries that participate in this program complicates and delays the process of resettlement. Resettlement is not the end of challenges that these young people might face throughout their protracted migration journey. Highly disrupted schooling and educational experiences as well as many other contextual challenges faced throughout the migration journey exacerbate the impact of post-resettlement barriers and hinder integration in their final country of resettlement.

Successful integration of young people is linked with many factors; educational pathways and meaningful employment are two of the key factors, both of which are central to career development. Addressing the career development of youth with refugee backgrounds is essential for improving outcomes related to these two factors and preventing negative social outcomes such as marginalisation and disengagement that exacerbate mental health issues. Assisting young people with refugee backgrounds with their career development – which is the focus of this research – is important due to the changing nature of the world of work in resettlement countries that presents new challenges for all citizens, especially young people with refugee backgrounds.

Career counselling is a specialised form of career development support. Therefore, career counsellors have an important role in assisting these young people with their career development. However, as there are many different approaches to career counselling, it is important to find a relevant approach to career counselling of young people with refugee backgrounds. As career development of young people with refugee backgrounds after resettlement is a largely neglected area of research, little is known about the nature of these young people’s career development and the relevance of certain career counselling approaches to assist them. For instance, narrative career counselling that relies on a client’s ability to tell career stories, has been proposed for career counselling of these young people after resettlement. However, whether young people with refugee backgrounds can access and tell career stories after resettlement has not been researched. This current thesis fills existing research gaps by investigating the career stories of young people who have been through a protracted migration journey. A better understanding about the career development of young people with refugee backgrounds through the exploration of their life-career stories, could provide useful information to career counsellors that may help them to enhance the relevance of their practice.

The findings of this research, result in a number of implications for career practice, theory, research and policy. Confirming the possibility of engaging young people with refugee backgrounds in narrative storytelling, suggests the potential relevance and usefulness of narrative approaches to career counselling that aim to facilitate self-reflection and enhancements of cultural and contextual self-understanding. Several considerations were proposed for career counsellors who work with this population. Preparatory strategies were suggested for qualitative researchers who work with vulnerable participants and are planning to step into the overlapping boundaries between narrative research and intervention practices. Potential contributions of the research, limitations and potential directions for future research were outlined.

title: Balance Sheet Decomposition of Crypto, CBDC, Stablecoin and RWA
affiliations: Fordham University - Graduate School of Arts & Sciences and Fordham University  - Department of Economics - Center for International Policy Studies (CIPS)

detail.title: Balance Sheet Decomposition of Crypto, CBDC, Stablecoin and RWA
detail.abstract: Cryptocurrencies, stablecoins, central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), and tokenized real-world assets (RWAs) are reshaping the balance sheets of central banks, commercial banks, non-bank financial intermediaries and households, yet existing literature examines them in isolation. This paper constructs the first unified, multi-entity balance sheet framework incorporating all four asset classes across a six-stage stylized evolution. We make three contributions. First, we reveal crossasset transmission channels that are invisible in single-asset studies, such as stablecoin runs propagating through money market funds into sovereign debt markets. Second, we show that permissioned and permissionless blockchain issuance produces fundamentally different balance sheet dynamics: neutral liability substitution in the former versus unbounded off-balance-sheet leverage in the latter, analogous to pre-2008 shadow banking vehicles. Third, we document a DeFi credit multiplier through which bank deposits, once tokenized and rehypothecated on-chain, generate multiple layers of credit beyond prudential regulation.

title: Equality of Opportunity and the Case for a Universal Child Allowance
affiliations: University of San Diego School of Law

detail.title: Equality of Opportunity and the Case for a Universal Child Allowance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

publicationDetails.detailsText: San Diego Legal Studies Paper No. 26-007
publicationDetails.journalName: University of San Diego Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The widespread popularity of equal opportunity ideals fuels strong public support for helping low-income children despite fierce debate over aid to adults. Yet key features of many current child benefit programs undermine that ideal, in part because policymakers muddy the waters with additional aims when crafting them. Programs for children get tangled up in disputes over aid to adults, undermining the goal of giving all children a fair shot at success. This Article untangles that knot by explicitly centering the child as the locus of our concern. Building on equal opportunity theory, it proposes a Universal Child Allowance (UCA) that provides unconditional, no-strings-attached cash grants to all children. Discarding work requirements means that the neediest children are no longer excluded, incorrectly deemed “at fault” for their plight; unrestricted cash allows parents to decide what their children need most. Notably, evidence from existing programs and past experiments suggests parents spend extra cash in ways that benefit their children and that they will not drop out of the labor force altogether or “blow” a UCA on themselves. 

At a time of heated polarization, the time is right to explore a UCA. Focusing on children avoids disputes that plague universal basic income proposals and reflects the renewed political focus on opportunities instead of outcomes. This comprehensive analysis of a UCA—the first in the law review literature—complements public policy work that advocates for such a benefit but does not address key design questions. Further, it contributes to scholarship on the tax and transfer system, poverty, and welfare by advancing our understanding of the relationship between a benefit program’s normative goals and structural design choices. And for both advocates and opponents of unconditional cash transfers, it offers a nuanced exploration of the debate surrounding welfare reform that promises a potential resolution of the enduring stalemate over restrictions on government aid.

title: When does Titling Informality lead to the Upgrading of Slums?

detail.title: When does Titling Informality lead to the Upgrading of Slums?

contentType.other: Policy paper written in fulfillment of the requirements for the degree of Master of Public Administration in International Development, Harvard Kennedy School.

detail.abstract:
This policy paper claims that formal and informal institutions should be taken into consideration when designing urban land-titling programs. This is true not only when granting titles, but also before and after such programs. Taking the experience of the largest land formalization program carried out in Peru by COFOPRI, this policy paper suggests that although the program was properly designed to map and legally recognize informal arrangements related with the allocation of land; COFOPRI overlooked other informal arrangements related with the use of land that led the formalized dwellings to become informal again. 

By qualitatively analyzing the existing formal and informal institutions in four squatter settlements in Lima, the author finds that much of the economic progress of a slum depends jointly on the following: 1) Informal institutions: Squatters’ organizations and plans after occupation occurs and title is issued. Squatters aim for government recognition and access to public services. When both demands are met, settlers’ informal institutions fine-tune towards aiming at doing business, getting jobs and leveraging capital. 2) Formal Institutions: Government recognition of slum and access to courts, police offices, microfinance institutions, municipality and property registration offices. Formal institutions shape the informal ones. When they are absent, informal institutions take on their responsibilities. When they are present, they must be fine-tuned to the informal ones to maintain the formalized land within formality and enhance the effects of the granting of title deeds. 

COFOPRI should coordinate the provision of the fine-tuned formal institutions and quality public services to the slums with the respective public and private agencies, as well as with community representatives. These policy measures would be: 1) Political supportable: The Peruvian population perceives COFOPRI as one of the most reliable government agencies. The proposed policies are grounded on the local necessities in the slums, and there are no major veto players. 2) Administrative feasible: COFOPRI already has expertise dealing with informal organizations. It needs to organize internally to be able to both identify which slums lack the most of access to formal institutions and public services and coordinate their provision. 3) Technically correct, because the expected economic benefits of carrying out land titling programs considering the relevance of informal and formal institutions would exceed the required additional budget.

title: How Markets Forecast and "Front Run" Information: Bayesian Market Efficiency

detail.title: How Markets Forecast and "Front Run" Information: Bayesian Market Efficiency

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: A common and widely accepted conclusion in rational expectations models of financial reporting is that a scheduled report (e.g., the annual company earnings statement) can not affect the firm's stock price or cost of capital until the result is reported. I argue that Bayesian investors, rather than waiting, infer a probability distribution over what might be in the report and re-price the stock based on that probability distribution. To allow for their uncertainty about the report's content and the resulting stock price, the asset pricing formula includes a risk premium related strictly to the precision or quality of the firm's financial reporting. That premium can be positive or negative, which means that the firm can affect its cost of capital up or down by its choice of information system.

title: Bankruptcy Law, Creditor Rights, and Earnings Management in Distressed Indian Firms
affiliations: , Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, Powai, Mumbai, India and SUNY College at Brockport

detail.title: Bankruptcy Law, Creditor Rights, and Earnings Management in Distressed Indian Firms
detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of creditor rights on earnings management practices of financially distressed firms in India. Using the enactment of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) 2016 as a quasi-experiment and applying a difference-indifferences design, we investigate how enhanced creditor rights, resulting from this new bankruptcy regulation, affect the earnings management behaviours of financially distressed firms. We find that these firms significantly increase their income-increasing earnings management activities post-IBC implementation. We also document that the post-IBC increases in earnings management are less salient in firms with better corporate governance quality and also smaller among family firms than non-family firms. Our results remain robust across alternative measures and different estimation models. We reveal that bankruptcy law reforms influence managerial reporting incentives and highlight the roles of corporate governance and ownership structure in mitigating managerial opportunism and safeguarding creditor rights for listed and unlisted distressed firms in India.

title: A Multi-method Econometric Analysis of SME Loan's Impacts on Women's Entrepreneurial Development in Bangladesh
affiliations: Bangladesh Institute of Capital Market , University of Dhaka and University of Dhaka

detail.title: A Multi-method Econometric Analysis of SME Loan's Impacts on Women's Entrepreneurial Development in Bangladesh

declarations.ethicsApproval: Written consent is properly taken while doing survey with questionnaire. Apart from that, no ethical issues are concerned.

detail.abstract: The paper examines how the socioeconomic developments of women entrepreneurs in Bangladesh are influenced by small and medium enterprises (SMEs). An equal weighted composite index based on a quantitative cross-sectional survey design was employed on 489 women entrepreneurs borrowing SME loans to meet the objectives. The study employed methodologies such as OLS, quantile regression, bootstrapped regression, standardised beta regression, hierarchical regression, and moderation effects to test the hypotheses and check the robustness. Results indicate that access to loans and adequacy of loans have a positive influence on the socioeconomic development of women entrepreneurs. On the other hand, tight credit checks, excessive collateral requirements and lack of institutional support are growth inhibitors, particularly among lowincome individuals. The study has significant policy implications in that SME loans are significantly contributing to the socioeconomic welfare of the women entrepreneurs, and Loan factors impact mostly, while both age and education imply the variations across the benefits received from the SME loans. This paper adds value to the literature by examining the dynamics between financial inclusion and institutional support in determining the success of women entrepreneurs by leveraging rigorous econometric modelling. The study paves the way to further research and policy development with a focus on the absorption of SME benefits by optimising loan factors and institutional factors, similar to other emerging economies.

title: Expected value‑added, employment, and climate impacts of an offshore Carbon Capture Storage system in Denmark
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, DTU Management, Technical University of Denmark and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Joint Program on the Science and Policy of Global Change

detail.title: Expected value‑added, employment, and climate impacts of an offshore Carbon Capture Storage system in Denmark

keywords: Keywords: Offshore carbon capture and storage (CCS)

detail.abstract: The economic and environmental co-benefits of offshore carbon capture and storage (CCS) infrastructure remain largely unquantified at the project level. This study provides the first economy-wide appraisal of a planned Danish offshore CCS system—the BIFROST project—which repurposes existing North Sea hydrocarbon pipelines and depleted reservoirs for permanent geological CO₂ storage. A bottom-up cost inventory covering liquefaction, shipping, pipeline transport, and offshore injection, validated through semi-structured interviews with industry experts, is integrated into a multi-regional input–output (MRIO) model to trace direct and indirect effects on value added (VA), employment, and greenhouse gas emissions across global supply chains. Over a 28-year, three-phase lifetime storing approximately 190 Mt of CO₂, the project generates €1.5–1.6 billion in global VA and 110,000–117,000 job-years, of which €0.4–0.5 billion and 14,000–24,000 job-years accrue to Denmark. Upstream and on-site CO₂ emissions (Scopes 2 and 3) represent 9.3–10.5% of the volume permanently stored; sourcing liquefaction power from low-carbon grids emerges as the most effective lever for reducing this ratio. Two transport sequences are compared: Denmark's domestic returns are maximised when pipeline transport is adopted as early as possible and liquefaction facilities are sited domestically. These findings indicate that repurposed offshore infrastructure can deliver simultaneous climate mitigation and regional economic gains when transport sequencing, plant siting, and fiscal policy are jointly optimised.

title: Unveiling Agricultural Resilience to Climate Change: A Structural Model Analysis Using Australian Farm Data Abstract
affiliations: and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Unveiling Agricultural Resilience to Climate Change: A Structural Model Analysis Using Australian Farm Data Abstract
detail.abstract: Understanding the impact of weather shocks on agricultural production and farmers’ adaptive capacity is critical for designing effective climate policies. This paper develops a structural model to examine farmers’ profit-maximizing responses to weather variability, distinguishing between output transformation and input adaptation effects. Using longitudinal data from broadacre farms in New South Wales, Australia (1977–2007), we find that water scarcity, rather than temperature fluctuations, poses the most significant constraint on farm productivity. A 1% decline in rainfall reduces crop production by 0.5% and livestock production by 0.1%. Each millimeter decrease in annual rainfall reduces annual farm profits by AU$8,700. While input adjustments help mitigate losses, adaptive strategies differ by farm type and regional conditions, with livestock producers in arid zones demonstrating greater flexibility. These findings underscore the importance of region-specific, production-tailored adaptation policies to strengthen agricultural resilience in the face of climate change.
