detail.abstract: In this paper, we propose a word and expression-level recognition system using Pose Estimation and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) for Myanmar Sign Language. The model converts Myanmar Sign Language from videos into Burmese words and expressions, using diverse data collected from different people in various situations for training. In the data preprocessing stage, the dataset was subjected to the landmark of face, body, and hand using mediapipe, with the resulting data stored as numpy arrays in CSV format. These arrays were subsequently used as the training data input for the model. The model's function involved predicting or recognizing the signs presented in the input video. The accuracy rate during the training phase was 94.4%, whereas the accuracy rate during the validation phase was slightly lower at 92.78%. A 60% accuracy rate was attained in the real-time testing phase using signer data that had not been seen before by the model. Whereas people who are new to studying sign language achieve an accuracy rate of 80% resulting in human performance remaining superior to the model. Our main purpose is to break the barrier and connect hearing-impaired people to hearing people with our research and technologies as much as possible. Lastly, we believe that our approach will help solve the problem of hearing-impaired people unable to communicate with hearing people.

title: Economic Impact Analysis of Public-Charging Tariff Reduction on Electric Vehicle Adoption in the UAE
affiliations: Hamdan Bin Mohammed Smart University, Hamdan Bin Mohammed Smart University and Hamdan Bin Mohammed Smart University

detail.title: Economic Impact Analysis of Public-Charging Tariff Reduction on Electric Vehicle Adoption in the UAE
detail.abstract: Under the United Arab Emirates (UAE) Net Zero 2050 strategic initiative, the nation aims to achieve a 50% adoption rate of electric vehicles (EVs). However, despite significant investment in charging infrastructure, current adoption rates remain below 5%, raising critical questions about the factors impeding this transition. This study investigates a fundamental barrier to EV adoption: the Dubai Electricity and Water Authority’s (DEWA) direct current (DC) fast-charging tariff of AED 1.26 per kilowatt-hour (kWh). This pricing structure renders the operation of EVs 35% more expensive than that of efficient internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles. A comparative analysis of 50 EV models reveals an average operating cost of AED 22.33 per 100 km, compared to AED 16.57 per 100 km for efficient petrol vehicles, creating a significant economic disincentive that disproportionately affects the 60% of Dubai residents residing in apartments who rely exclusively on public charging infrastructure. International benchmarking further indicates that the UAE’s charging-to-petrol cost ratio of 135% significantly exceeds that of successful markets, such as Norway (32%) and Finland (29%), where ratios between 20% and 50% have driven widespread adoption. Based on these findings, this study recommends reducing DC fast-charging tariffs to a range of AED 0.45–0.55/kWh. Such an adjustment would not only align energy costs with international best practices but also restore the economic rationale for EV ownership, enabling the realization of the UAE's national EV adoption targets and contributing to an estimated 26 million tonnes of annual carbon dioxide emissions reduction.

title: Dynamic Credit Risk Assessment under Carbon Transition Pressures: Evi-dence from Chinese Firms
affiliations: China Jiliang University, Monash University - Department of Econometrics & Business Statistics, Monash University - Department of Econometrics & Business Statistics and China Jiliang University

detail.title: Dynamic Credit Risk Assessment under Carbon Transition Pressures: Evi-dence from Chinese Firms
detail.abstract: The rapid transition to a low-carbon economy challenges traditional credit-risk assessment, especially in carbon-intensive industries. In this paper, we develop a dynamic framework that embeds carbon-transition exposure into corporate risk assessment. Sector-specific data en-velopment analysis treats total greenhouse gas emission intensity as a negative (undesirable) input, producing interpretable carbon cost signals. We separate historical from expected per-formance using maximum-entropy time weights and peer-incentive adjustments, then classify firms with a topology-aware self-organizing map followed by K-means clustering. For 1,222 Chinese listed firms across 11 sectors during 2016–2021, we find that: (i) carbon intensity is the second-most important driver of efficiency after leverage, with substantial cross-sector het-erogeneity; (ii) forward-looking scoring materially reorders mid-tier firms while the top and bottom deciles remain stable across reasonable settings of the time-preference parameter; and (iii) industries group into three patterns—history–expectation synchronization, expecta-tion-dominant, and history-oriented.

title: Policy Design and Firm-Level Energy Efficiency: Evidence from Emissions Trading versus Command-and-Control in Korea
affiliations: University of Seoul and University of Seoul

detail.title: Policy Design and Firm-Level Energy Efficiency: Evidence from Emissions Trading versus Command-and-Control in Korea
detail.abstract: This study investigates how differences in climate policy design—emissions trading versus command-and-control regulation—affect firm-level energy efficiency. Exploiting the coexistence of the Korea Emissions Trading Scheme and its command-and-control Target Management System, we identify the net effects of policy type on firms’ energy and carbon intensity. Using firm-level panel data from 2011 to 2023, we implement a staggered difference-in-differences framework and a separate event-study design to trace dynamic treatment effects. Because regime eligibility is determined by emissions thresholds, we focus on firms whose emissions lie in a neighborhood around the regulatory cutoffs and construct a unified measure of policy stringency to isolate policy-type effects. We find that emissions trading is associated with significant improvements in both energy and carbon intensity during the early phase of the Korea Emissions Trading Scheme, although these advantages diminished over time. Policy effects are stronger for firms with greater financial capacity, while target stringency alone does not guarantee sustained improvements. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of differentiated market-based policy design that accounts for firms’ financial conditions and sectoral abatement potential.

title: Brighten Life After Sunset: The Improvement on Mental Health From Nighttime Economy
affiliations: , Beijing Foreign Studies University, University of Colorado Denver and

detail.title: Brighten Life After Sunset: The Improvement on Mental Health From Nighttime Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: Mental health problems impose substantial social and economic burdens worldwide and call for innovative public strategies beyond conventional individual medical interventions. The nighttime economy in China has developed over the ages into a multifaceted paradigm that systematically combines outdoor social entertainment and small family businesses, a phenomenon rare in the West. This paper aims to explore the relationship between the development of the nighttime economy and mental health. With a dataset from the China Family Panel Survey (CFPS), we find that the development of the nighttime economy significantly improves residents' mental health. This positive effect exhibits a distinct social-equality orientation: it effectively benefits both low- and high-income groups but through heterogeneous channels that align with their respective needs. Specifically, the nighttime economy enhances low-income residents' mental health via the income channel, while improving high-income residents' mental health via the consumption channel. Geographical patterns further show that the gains are concentrated where baseline amenities are relatively scarce. In northern provinces, where the nighttime economy lags behind that of southern counterparts, favorable summer temperatures expand opportunities for evening outdoor activities, so increases in nighttime economic activity translate into larger improvements in mental health. Within provinces, the effects are stronger in rural than in urban areas, consistent with the idea that limited recreational alternatives leave greater scope for the nighttime economy to enhance well-being. These findings highlight the nighttime economy as an innovative socio-economic lever to promote population mental health, offering a complementary pathway to relieve healthcare burdens and foster inclusive growth.

title: Fairness and the SEC's Competing Regulatory Paradigms
affiliations: NYU Pollack Center for Law & Business

detail.title: Fairness and the SEC's Competing Regulatory Paradigms
detail.abstract:
The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has invoked fairness to justify trading restrictions in the stock market, particularly in the areas of insider trading, high-frequency trading, and short selling. The Commission typically includes fairness considerations in its cost-benefit analysis, reasoning that such restrictions enhance investors’ perceived fairness of the stock market, which in turn bolsters investor confidence, thereby promoting capital formation, market stability, and ultimately allocative efficiency. 

Invoking fairness as a policy justification, however, raises questions under the arbitrary-and-capricious standard of the Administrative Procedure Act, which requires the SEC to provide an adequate justification for its rules. Indeed, scholars have noted that, although the Commission has sometimes included perceived fairness in its cost-benefit analysis, it has not demonstrated empirically how certain trading restrictions generate measurable benefits in terms of enhanced perceived fairness and thereby allocative efficiency. This Article argues that such shortcomings reveal the limits of the “efficiency regulatory paradigm” as a framework for justifying fairness-based trading restrictions. This Article contends that, where feasible, the Commission should instead explain how such restrictions align with the principle of fair markets. Codified in Section 2 of the Exchange Act, this principle can be construed as justifying restrictions not only on trading practices that result in unfair prices but also on those that confer either undue advantages or lawful advantages that allow sophisticated investors to increase their wealth at the expense of individual investors without creating any meaningful social value. This approach recognizes the relevance of fairness within the “public values regulatory paradigm,” in which regulatory principles independent of efficiency can justify rulemaking for the equity market structure.

By examining short selling regulation as a case study, this Article demonstrates the SEC’s inadequate justification of trading restrictions as necessary to enhance perceived fairness and thereby allocative efficiency. At the same time, the short selling context illustrates how the Commission could instead ground such restrictions in the principle of fair markets, treated as an independent regulatory principle. Given the increased scrutiny by courts and interest groups regarding the SEC’s rulemaking justifications, this Article advances an analytical framework to guide both the SEC and policy analysts in articulating fairness as a defensible policy justification in securities regulation.

title: Fighting Fake News with Peer Feedback: Theory and Experiment
affiliations: Waseda University, Waseda University, Hitotsubashi University - Graduate School of Economics and Waseda University - Graduate School of Economics

detail.title: Fighting Fake News with Peer Feedback: Theory and Experiment
detail.abstract: The diffusion of fake news on social media poses a growing challenge to society. This study develops a theoretical model and laboratory experiment to examine whether userto-user feedback such as likes or negative comments can reduce fake news sharing. We construct a sender-receiver game in which the sender receives a signal from potentially unreliable sources and decides whether to share it, while feedback from the receiver enables learning about information quality over time. The model predicts that (i) peer feedback induces self-selection: individuals with unreliable sources learn to stop sharing, and (ii) fake news spreads more when senders are motivated by reputation rather than accuracy, though this effect is modest. We test these predictions by developing a novel lab experiment based on the ball-and-urn experimental design. Consistent with the theory, feedback reduces fake news sharing, but effects are weaker due to underreaction in belief updating and noisy decisions. Differences across motivational incentives are minimal. These findings highlight both the potential and limits of peer feedback in preventing fake news sharing, offering implications for platforms seeking to curb misinformation through user-to-user feefback.

title: Reforming Tax or Reshaping Rights? A Critical Analysis of the Income Tax Bill, 2025
affiliations: Amity University, Amity Law School

detail.title: Reforming Tax or Reshaping Rights? A Critical Analysis of the Income Tax Bill, 2025
detail.abstract: The new Income Tax Bill is drafted to replace the Income Tax Act, 1961, with a more up-to-date and organized system. The bill makes procedures simpler and increases the use of technology, but it has raised serious concerns about its strong surveillance. The study examines if Sections of the bill are in line with the Constitution such as the right to privacy mentioned in Article 21 and the distribution of powers mentioned in Articles 246 and 280. Judging from tax practices in the United States, United Kingdom and Canada, the paper finds what works best and where Indian laws deviate from democratic rules in other nations. In the end, it is recognized that without proper judicial review, strong statutory safeguards and adequate federal regulations, the bill might challenge civil liberties and the balance between state and federal governments. The paper gives specific proposals for tax reform that are in line with what the Constitution and international laws require.

title: The Contract-Based Approach To Restructuring Sovereign Debt: Theory, Evolution, And Reform
affiliations: Centre for International Governance Innovation and Harvard Law School

detail.title: The Contract-Based Approach To Restructuring Sovereign Debt: Theory, Evolution, And Reform
detail.abstract: This Paper presents a new theoretical framework for understanding how insolvent foreign nation-states work out their defaulted debts. "Sovereign debt restructuring," as the process is known, is of critical importance to the dozens of developing countries around the world who have borrowed over 1 trillion dollars under the law of the State of New York and other jurisdictions. It explains how and why the prevailing system of sovereign debt restructuring works even though it operates informally and is based on voluntary, out-of-court negotiations supported by the inclusion of voting clauses in sovereign bonds to bind-in holdout creditors ("Collective Action Clauses"). The theory of sovereign debt restructuring is introduced through a review of the famous 2001 and 2003 policy debates (known as "the CAC-SDRM debate") that pitted the U.S. Treasury, which favored the voluntary, contract-based approach based approach that is used today against the International Monetary Fund ("I.M.F."), which favored the adoption of a formal, treaty-based, Chapter-11-like statutory scheme, which it called a Sovereign Debt Restructuring Mechanism ("SDRM"). Material from these debates plus additional insights borrowed from the theory of corporate insolvency, the doctrine of sovereign immunity, and financial history are then used to argue that a workable system must be based on the voluntary participation of the sovereign and other stakeholder groups. This Paper sets out design principles for designing a workable voluntary sovereign debt restructuring system and presents a model of how the various parties and processes are effectively coordinated. This Paper concludes with the proposal of two incremental reforms to help fill observed gaps in the prevailing system: (i) an expansion of existing statutory stay powers to limit to the potential for disruption of out-of-court negotiations brought by uncooperative creditors; and (ii) a limitation on payment-blocking injunctions like the one granted in the Argentina bond litigation that led to a fresh default on 30 billion dollars of performing, but previously-restructured bonds.

title: Production Network Spillovers from EU Funded R&D Grants
affiliations: University of Dubrovnik,  and

detail.title: Production Network Spillovers from EU Funded R&D Grants

declarations.funderStatement: This study was supported by the Croatian Science Foundation under project IP-2022-10-8560.

detail.abstract: Firms are embedded in production networks, so the returns to innovation policy may extend far beyond direct recipients. We quantify upstream propagation of R&D grants using administrative data from Croatia's €200 million program and comprehensive firm-to-firm transaction records. Grants generate large direct effects: recipient revenue rises by about 17%, material costs by about 22%, employment by about 8%, and tangible assets by about 27%. These gains transmit strongly to suppliers. Exposed suppliers expand persistently, with revenue increasing by roughly 28-46% and material costs by roughly 30-51%; employment rises more modestly but durably (about 9-12% from year 1 onward), while tangible assets accumulate gradually (roughly 17-40% over years 1-4). Spillovers are strongest for geographically proximate ties but remain meaningful well beyond local relationships. They accrue disproportionately to smaller firms and are more pronounced among financially constrained suppliers. Accounting for supplier responses raises the implied total impact to about four times the direct recipient effect. Production networks are therefore central to assessing the economic returns to innovation policy.

title: Treasury Financing by Hedge Funds: A Tale of Three Channels
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Isenberg School of Management and

detail.title: Treasury Financing by Hedge Funds: A Tale of Three Channels
detail.abstract: Hedge funds have become critical players in Treasury markets. To finance large amounts of Treasuries, hedge funds borrow in the repo market from commercial banks and dealers. We identify three channels that affect hedge fund borrowing costs. First, repo supply is inelastic, with larger Treasury offerings leading to higher repo rates paid by hedge funds (fiscal channel). Second, commercial banks reduce repo supply when their reserves decline (monetary channel). Lastly, bank leverage constraints increase the costs of repo intermediation, which are passed on to hedge funds as higher repo funding costs (regulatory channel).

title: Risk Sensing: LLMs for Risk Monitoring in SME Lending

detail.title: Risk Sensing: LLMs for Risk Monitoring in SME Lending
detail.abstract:
Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are central to global economies yet face persistent credit constraints due to limited reliable financial data. This paper introduces RiskSensing, a dual-LLM agentic framework that extracts actionable credit risk signals from unstructured customer interaction records (chat transcripts and profiles) in digital banking channels. The framework consists of two core modules: (1) an LLM-augmented customer graph discovery pipeline that uncovers hidden person-to-business and business-to-business connections, and (2) an LLM-driven risk signal detection agent that identifies adverse events (operational disruptions, legal issues, bankruptcy signals, and key-person risks) using a custom risk taxonomy and structured prompting.

Deployed in the SME credit portfolio monitoring at a digital bank, the framework increased detection coverage by 23% (hidden connections) and 25% (adverse events, pooled across cohorts) over traditional baselines (company registries and third-party news feeds). Borrowers flagged by hidden connection signals showed 2.3× higher subsequent delinquency rates; those flagged by adverse event signals showed 2.4× higher rates. The median lead time from signal detection to delinquency was three months. Qualitative expert review confirmed high operational relevance.

The study demonstrates that customer conversational data, when processed through a modular LLM architecture, provides timely and complementary risk intelligence that traditional structured sources cannot capture. Practical implementation considerations and performance metrics are discussed across the credit risk lifecycle.

title: Moral Hazard and Adverse Selection in the Social Insurance Market for Entrepreneurs
affiliations: University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB) - Department of Economics, Tampere University, VATT Institute for Economic Research, Tampere University and University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB)

detail.title: Moral Hazard and Adverse Selection in the Social Insurance Market for Entrepreneurs
detail.abstract: This paper studies social insurance contribution choices, adverse selection, and moral hazard among Finnish entrepreneurs. We exploit quasi-exogenous variation from a reform that relaxed mandatory contribution requirements for a subset of entrepreneurs, combining administrative registry data with linked survey evidence. Entrepreneurs who gained discretion reduced their contributions by 16%, on average, relative to entrepreneurs subject to a strict mandate. Using this variation, causal tests of anticipatory responses and moral hazard as well as positive correlation tests, we show that moral hazard and adverse selection effects are near zero in this market. Survey responses help illuminate the mechanisms underlying these results.

title: Not All Data Should Be Recovered: When Imputing Degrades Statistical Inference
affiliations: Tarleton State University and The University of Texas at Tyler

detail.title: Not All Data Should Be Recovered: When Imputing Degrades Statistical Inference
detail.abstract: In quantitative social science, the default response to empty cells is singular: impute. This practice ignores an ontological distinction between accidental absence (data the researcher failed to collect) and designed absence (data the researcher intentionally excluded to preserve experimental validity). We demonstrate that applying imputation to designed absence is a category error that systematically degrades inference. Using a large-scale discrete choice study (N = 7,181), we benchmark seven imputation methods, ranging from simple mean substitution to gradient-boosted Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE), against a ground-truth model estimated on observed data alone. Every method increased AIC, reduced predictive accuracy, and induced substantial coefficient bias. Most critically, imputation collapsed the variance structure, hollowing out the random effect and reducing the intraclass correlation (ICC) from a baseline of .602 to as low as .057. We demonstrate that "MICE" is not a singular method but a family of divergent models; on identical data, different MICE base learners produced contradictory substantive findings. The damage is driven by three mechanisms: counterfactual fabrication, de-randomization of experimental treatments, and the forced imposition of ergodicity on non-ergodic human behavior. We propose a new taxonomy of absence and argue that when data are absent by construction, the most defensible analytical response is to respect the design. No level of algorithmic sophistication can recover information from cells that were never intended to contain any.

title: From Transition to Physical Risk: Rethinking Portfolio Management
affiliations: Roma Tre University and Amundi Asset Management

detail.title: From Transition to Physical Risk: Rethinking Portfolio Management
detail.abstract:
Over the past fifteen years, responsible investment has evolved, shifting from broad ESG scores to more granular climate risk management. Transition risk has dominated, with portfolio decarbonization anchored in standardized carbon intensity metrics and, more recently, complemented by measures of green intensity. Frameworks such as the comprehensive integrated and core-satellite approaches now give investors effective tools to integrate transition risks into portfolio construction. In contrast, physical climate risk remains underdeveloped. Rising extreme weather events, chronic temperature increases, and ecosystem disruptions are already affecting asset values and supply chains. However, there is no standardized equivalent to carbon or green intensity for benchmarking. 

This paper argues that physical climate risk must now receive the same attention as transition risk. Unlike transition risk, physical climate risk lacks clear anchor metrics. This methodological gap explains why portfolio optimization that incorporates physical risk is still in its infancy. We review transition and physical risk modeling and discuss approaches for constructing physical risk scores. We also examine how to integrate these scores into portfolio optimization and strategic asset allocation. Our analysis shows that achieving significant reductions in both exposure and vulnerability to physical climate risk is extremely challenging. Moreover, the high shadow price associated with these mitigation policies suggests substantial implementation costs and trade-offs. Overall, we conclude that incorporating physical climate risk into portfolio management is considerably more complex than managing transition risk.

title: Large Effects of Small Cues: Priming Selfish Economic Decisions
affiliations: Bar-Ilan University, Bar-Ilan University, Texas A&M University - Department of Marketing, University of Iowa and

detail.title: Large Effects of Small Cues: Priming Selfish Economic Decisions

declarations.ethicsApproval: The project was approved by the Ethics Review Board (ERB) of the Economics Department of Bar-Ilan University.
declarations.funderStatement: No Funding Was Received.

detail.abstract: We use survey experiments to demonstrate that manipulating participants’ perceptions of the context can affect their decisions. We ran three survey experiments in the U.S. and Israel with participants from both economics and non-economics majors. In the experiments, participants face a tradeoff between profit maximization (market norm) and workers’ welfare (social norm). Our experimental setup enables us to discriminate between the self-selection and indoctrination effects. Existing studies find that economics and non-economics students make different choices in such situations, which the studies argue is because of differences in personality traits between economics students and others. While such differences might exist, we argue that context also plays an important role. Using priming to manipulate the context, we demonstrate that when participants receive cues signaling that their decision has an economic context, both economics and non-economics students tend to maximize profits. When participants receive cues emphasizing social norms, on the other hand, both economics and non-economics students are less likely to maximize profits. We find that the role of context in determining behavior is at least as large as the baseline differences between economics and non-economics students.

title: Group Identity and Cooperation in Infinitely Repeated Games
affiliations: Southern Methodist University (SMU), University of Arkansas and Tsinghua University

detail.title: Group Identity and Cooperation in Infinitely Repeated Games

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no competing interests and no additional funding sources to declare beyond those noted in the Funder Statement.
declarations.ethicsApproval: IRB approvals were obtained at the University of Texas-Dallas (#MR 11-079) and the University of Arkansas (Protocol #2405542458).
declarations.funderStatement: Li gratefully acknowledges the financial support provided by the University of Arkansas and the University of Texas-Dallas. Liu gratefully acknowledges financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China (72222005, 72342032). Financial support from NSFC (Grant No. 72573051) for Chen is also gratefully acknowledged.

detail.abstract:
We develop a theoretical framework and conduct a laboratory experiment to study how group identity affects cooperative behavior and strategy selection in infinitely repeated prisoner's dilemma (IRPD) games. We find that participants are more likely to cooperate and less likely to adopt the Always Defect strategy with ingroup members than with outgroup members or participants in the control condition. Ingroup pairs are also more likely to sustain cooperation but less likely to persist in defection over the dynamic course across supergames, compared to both outgroup and control pairs. However, these effects are statistically significant only in the low strategic risk environment when the discount factor is high enough for cooperation to be both a subgame perfect Nash equilibrium and risk dominant. In the high strategic risk environment where cooperation is
a subgame perfect Nash equilibrium but not risk dominant, the impact of group identity on cooperation is less robust and only holds qualitatively.

title: The 2024 Nobel Laureates Are Not Only Wrong About China, But Also About the West
affiliations: Johns Hopkins University

detail.title: The 2024 Nobel Laureates Are Not Only Wrong About China, But Also About the West
detail.abstract: Yuen Yuen Ang argues that the 2024 Nobel laureates in economics—Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson, and James Robinson—offer an outdated and overly simplistic theory of development. She agrees that institutions matter, but criticizes their tendency to equate “good” institutions with Western liberal democracies while ignoring colonial violence, slavery, extraction, and inequality in the rise of wealthy Western states. Using the United States as an example, she contends that prosperity was built not only on democracy and property rights, but also on dispossession, coerced labor, and elite privilege. Ang also rejects the laureates’ explanation of China’s growth as a temporary anomaly or the product of luck. Instead, she argues that China’s post-Mao reforms created partial accountability and bureaucratic adaptability within an authoritarian system, enabling rapid development without Western-style democracy. Overall, she calls for a less ideological, less Western-centric understanding of development and a more realistic defense of democracy’s value.

title: Generative AI-assisted Teaching Strategies for Designing Cost Structures With Rigor and Scalability
affiliations: , Universidad Metropolitana and Centro de Investigación y de Estudios Avanzados

detail.title: Generative AI-assisted Teaching Strategies for Designing Cost Structures With Rigor and Scalability

publicationDetails.detailsText: New literacies in the age of AI: Ethics, teaching, and writing (English Version)

detail.abstract: This chapter examines how to rigorously and scalably integrate generative artificial intelligence into the teaching of cost structures in higher education. The objective is to design a teaching framework and strategy architecture with prompts aimed at strengthening accounting reasoning, traceability, and formative assessment. An evidence-based instructional design approach is adopted that articulates active learning, supervised algorithmic tutoring, and verification protocols. Additionally, prototypes are proposed for activity-based costing, time-based extensions, and cost-volume-profit analysis, along with prompt engineering rubrics and learning outcome matrices. The findings point to significant improvements in process transparency, the relevance of assumptions, and the reasoned defense of decisions when these are based on the documentation of interactions, triangulating product, process, and calculation. It is also noted that quality depends on data curation, critical literacy, and meaningful human oversight. The implementation of responsible use policies, the creation of curriculum-aligned prompt libraries, and the development of assessment cycles with iterative feedback are recommended. The contribution lies in translating the current discussion on generative AI into operational practices that enhance the quality of learning (SDG4) and the reliability of accounting decisions.

title: Flora, Fauna, and Fairness: Reframing Financial Risk as Ecological Responsibility
affiliations: University of Melbourne - Department of Finance, Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT University), University of Melbourne - School of Botany, University of Melbourne, Cambridge Judge Business School - Finance Subject Group, FTSE Russell, London Stock Exchange Group, SKEMA Business School and University of Melbourne

detail.title: Flora, Fauna, and Fairness: Reframing Financial Risk as Ecological Responsibility
detail.abstract: This commentary examines the ethical implications of biodiversity measurement in corporate finance. We argue that the lack of epistemic clarity—the inability to see the specific, spatial consequences of corporate action—is the primary obstacle to ethical biodiversity stewardship. Drawing on the concept of moral decoupling, we contend that this abstraction into simplified financial risk metrics allows decision-makers to overlook the specific ecological consequences of their value chains. We propose that the next generation of biodiversity metrics must move beyond the financialized aggregation of the nature-as-asset paradigm towards spatial resolution. Using the nSTAR methodology as a case study, we demonstrate how spatially explicit tools can serve as Moral Technologies that restore the link between corporate action and ecological reality. By improving the resolution of measurement, these tools provide the necessary epistemic foundation for genuine stewardship and accountability. We conclude that adopting such high-resolution tools is a moral imperative, as they collapse the distance between the boardroom and the biosphere, restoring the capacity for accountability in an age of extinction.

title: Generative Feedback: Causal Effects of LLM’s on Writing Quality and Evaluative Equity in Higher Education
affiliations: , Universidad Metropolitana, Centro de Investigación y de Estudios Avanzados and Centro de Investigación y de Estudios Avanzados

detail.title: Generative Feedback: Causal Effects of LLM’s on Writing Quality and Evaluative Equity in Higher Education
detail.abstract: This chapter examines, within the framework of SDG 4, how large-scale generative feedback using large language models (LLMs) impacts the quality of scholarly writing and evaluative equity in higher education. The aim is to estimate improvements in coherence, argumentation, use of evidence, and clarity, and to determine whether gaps between subgroups (L1/L2, first generation, and baseline performance) are reduced. An experimental or quasi-experimental design (stepped-wedge cluster trial) with blinded assessment based on analytical rubrics and secondary metrics such as time to feedback, revision iterations, editing distance, self-efficacy, and teaching load is recommended. A synthesis of recent evidence suggests consistent gains when LLM feedback is effectively integrated into explicit rubrics and revision microtasks; furthermore, it increases engagement and can decrease inter-rater variability. However, risks of dependency, stylistic homogenization, and algorithmic bias are noted. Therefore, this chapter proposes a framework for didactic governance with traceability (registration of prompts, versions, and logs), open science principles (pre-registration, repositories), and a dual humanAI evaluation scheme with bias audits and human-in-the-loop thresholds. Among the limitations acknowledged are the heterogeneity of contexts, sensitivity to model versions, and external validity. The conclusion is that, under ethical safeguards and with teacher training, generative feedback can raise writing standards and broaden inclusion; further research is suggested on differential effects, disciplinary transferability, and institutional sustainability of scaling up.

title: Into the Great Wide Open: Restructuring the Dana Gas Sukuk Outside of the Confines of the Universalist and Territorialist Frameworks

detail.title: Into the Great Wide Open: Restructuring the Dana Gas Sukuk Outside of the Confines of the Universalist and Territorialist Frameworks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This is an original work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This article is not based on a study with patients/participants.
declarations.funderStatement: The research for this article was independently funded.

detail.abstract:
Dana Gas PJSC, a Public Joint Stock Company incorporated under the laws of the United Arab Emirates, was founded in 2005 and was the first and largest regional private sector natural gas company in the Middle East. Its shares traded on the Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange and drew much investment in the company's gas exploration initiatives.  Then there was a problem timely repaying in full a US $1 billion issuance of certificates that were listed on the Irish Stock Exchange and due for redemption on 31 October 2017. 

In a strategy that bankers at Houlihan Lokey are credited with suggesting - Dana Gas took the stance that it could not repay its debt because doing so would not be Sharia compliant.  Dana Gas challenged the legality of its debt issuances under Islamic finance law, thereby also disputing Dana Gas had a repayment obligation.  

The controversial stance roiled Islamic financial markets, including the market for issuances of Sukuk sometimes referred to in slang as Islamic bonds.  

The markets adjusted and settled down.  And from what I recall, though it has been several years now, there was a happy ending for Dana Gas' debt issuance.  After getting embroiled in costly, time-consuming legal proceedings in the UK and UAE, the company was paid by good customers that had been slow-paying for gas such as governments, and there were other favorable developments on the gas exploration/business end.  So it was possible for Dana Gas to repay nervous investors while having others continue to be invested in the success of the company on new terms.  
  
Dana Gas remains an interesting case study because there are a lot of contracts under combinations of English law and Sharia law.  There haven't been examples of courts in multiple jurisdictions cooperating in an insolvency scenario governed by multiple choices of law, concerning hundreds of millions or billions of dollars in asset value, with the exception of rare cases like Arcapita Bank where there were concurrent proceedings in the courts of the Cayman Islands and the Southern District of New York.

title: Ring-Fencing and Heterogeneity of Credit Distribution
affiliations: Bank of England, University of Leicester School of Business and Bank of England

detail.title: Ring-Fencing and Heterogeneity of Credit Distribution
detail.abstract: This paper provides the first comprehensive evidence on the distributional effects of the UK ringfencing regulation on mortgage credit allocation and pricing. Introduced after the Global Financial Crisis and fully implemented in 2019, ring-fencing required large banking groups to separate core retail activities from investment banking operations, reshaping funding structures and lending incentives. Using a unique dataset of over 13 million mortgages granted between 2010 and 2024, we examine how ring-fencing affected mortgage spreads, lending standards, and access to credit across borrower groups and market segments. Consistent with prior research, we document an aggregate decline in mortgage spreads following the reform. However, we show that these reductions were disproportionately larger for young borrowers and households in economically deprived regions, indicating a significant reduction in risk premia for traditionally disadvantaged groups. We also find that ring-fenced banks increased their tolerance for higher loan-to-value lending, particularly in the first-time buyer segment. During the cost-of-living crisis, ring-fenced banks absorbed a greater share of funding cost shocks for borrowers in disadvantaged areas. Overall, our findings demonstrate that structural banking reform can materially affect not only financial stability and pricing, but also the distribution of credit and inequality in housing finance.

title: A Post-Growth Deal for Italy: Exploring the Coalition-Building Potential of Non-Reformist Reforms
affiliations: Autonomous University of Barcelona, University of Urbino, Autonomous University of Barcelona and Autonomous University of Barcelona

detail.title: A Post-Growth Deal for Italy: Exploring the Coalition-Building Potential of Non-Reformist Reforms
detail.abstract: Challenging green growth narratives, degrowth argues that achieving ecological sustainability in high-income countries requires a democratically planned and socially just downscaling of production and consumption, alongside a reorientation of economic institutions toward collective wellbeing within planFetary boundaries. While post-growth and degrowth scholarship has increasingly shifted from critique to policy proposals, limited attention has been paid to the political agency and coalition-building capacity required to implement such policies. This paper asks whether a post-growth policy package can function as an emancipatory tool for building a counter-hegemonic alliance capable of contesting growth-dependent capitalism. We examine perceptions of a ”Post-Growth Deal” composed of five non-reformist reforms – Universal Care Income (UCI), Universal Public Services (UPS), Working Time Reduction (WTR), a Public Job Guarantee (PJG), and Deliberative Forums (DF) – among three strategically positioned actor groups: environmental activists, labor union members, and progressive political party members. Using a mixed-methods approach that combines focus group discussions with a survey, we analyze the desirability, communicability, achievability, and perceived popularity of these measures. Our findings show that work-centered policies, particularly WTR and a PJG, display the strongest potential for cross-group alignment, while more redistributive and participatory measures face greater ideological and communicative barriers. The study contributes to ecological economics by empirically assessing the coalition-building potential of post-growth policies, foregrounding compromise and political strategy, and situating degrowth debates within a southern European context, focussing on the case-study of Italy.

title: Relative Cost Competitiveness and Relative Export Performance in the Euro Area
affiliations: University of the German Federal Armed Forces - Helmut Schmidt Universität

detail.title: Relative Cost Competitiveness and Relative Export Performance in the Euro Area

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: I show how internal price and cost divergences within the euro area translate into export outcomes when competitiveness is inherently relative. I develop a transparent peer-based framework that links a Relative Price Competitiveness (RPC) indicator-measuring domestic prices or costs relative to a fixed group of core euroarea peers-to a matching Relative Export Performance (REP) measure defined as export growth relative to the same peer group. The analysis covers intra-euro, extra-euro, and total exports for France, Germany, Italy, and Spain using quarterly data since 2000. Empirically, I combine country-specific regressions with country-level and pooled local projection methods to assess both contemporaneous and dynamic relationships. My results show that relative price competitiveness is a robust and economically meaningful determinant of relative export performance inside and outside the eurozone, while its link with absolute export growth is weaker and more heterogeneous across countries. These findings underscore the usefulness of a relative framework for isolating internal competitiveness effects in a monetary union, beyond what can be inferred from real effective exchange rates or export growth alone.

title: Carbon Uncertainty and Asset Prices
affiliations: University of Glasgow, Adam Smith Business School, University of Chicago - Booth School of Business,  and EDHEC Business School

detail.title: Carbon Uncertainty and Asset Prices
detail.abstract: We find that measurement uncertainty in firms’ carbon intensity commands a positive risk premium, distinct from and alongside a robust premium associated with carbon-intensity levels. Because most emissions are estimated rather than disclosed, our main contribution is to construct an observation-level measure of carbon-data precision at scale: for each firm-month, we quantify the uncertainty of the underlying carbon signal. We conceptually separate estimation risk (statistical error from inferring emissions under sparse firm information) from model risk, proxied by cross-vendor disagreement. Using a replicable Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE) framework combined with Random Forests, we jointly estimate firm-month emissions, carbon intensity, and uncertainty for the full CRSP universe, overcoming the selection bias inherent in vendor-restricted samples. Training on self-disclosing firms, we show that vendor-estimated data are largely redundant: adding vendor observations provides little incremental information beyond disclosures, consistent with estimates being anchored to the same disclosure backbone. By contrast, imputations within vendor-covered universes can embed selection bias and materially alter asset-pricing inferences. Overall, investors price not only carbon exposure but also carbon opacity.

title: Green investment support measures: a multi-sectoral, macro-financial analysis for the European Union
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Green investment support measures: a multi-sectoral, macro-financial analysis for the European Union
detail.abstract: The transition to a low-carbon economy requires substantial investment to replace the production technologies and infrastructure reliant on fossil fuels. In addition to regulation and carbon pricing, a range of financial policies has been proposed to accelerate green investment. This article evaluates the implications of three of them — direct green investment subsidies, green public guarantees, and capital market deepening — in terms of emission reduction, economic activity, and public debt. The analysis relies on a stock-flow consistent, input-output model of the EU economy, which explicitly incorporates industries’ marginal abatement costs, intersectoral input-output linkages, and investment financing channels. Model simulations reveal that direct subsidies are the most effective tool for achieving significant emission reductions; however, they also result in substantial increases in the debt-to-GDP ratio. In contrast, public guarantees and equity market development tend to strengthen public finances and economic activity but yield only moderate emission cuts. The results further suggest that combining policies can effectively balance emission mitigation and economic activity without compromising public finance sustainability.

title: Reverse Breakup Fees and Antitrust Approval
affiliations: University of Michigan Law School and University of Texas at Austin - School of Law

detail.title: Reverse Breakup Fees and Antitrust Approval
detail.abstract: The paper examines the antitrust implications of use of reverse breakup (termination) fees in mergers. By promising to pay a reverse breakup fee to the target if the proposed merger does not get the necessary antitrust approval, the acquirer can signal to the antitrust authority that the merger is more likely to be pro-competitive. A large reverse breakup fee can also function as a commitment device by the acquirer to spend more resources in case the merger is challenged by the antitrust authority. While the first, signaling function is efficiency enhancing, the second, commitment function can lead to an efficiency loss. The paper examines the various conditions under which a reverse breakup fee can serve these two functions and also derives welfare and policy implications.

title: Algorithmic Anchoring: How Prompt-Embedded Reference Points Bias LLM Financial Estimates

detail.title: Algorithmic Anchoring: How Prompt-Embedded Reference Points Bias LLM Financial Estimates
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in financial analysis; however, it remains unclear whether numerical cues embedded in prompts systematically bias their outputs. This study conducts a controlled equity-valuation experiment using fictional companies that minimize firmspecific training-data priors and hold fundamentals constant. Across 51,000 API invocations of three commercial models (Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-5-mini, and Gemini 2.5 Flash), I randomize prompt-embedded anchors and estimate how valuations and downstream outputs respond. Three findings emerge. First, source framing amplifies anchoring: labeling the same number as a prior AI estimate increases valuation sensitivity to the anchor by 52% (slope 0.272 to 0.413), consistent with greater weight placed on a source-labeled prior rather than greater numeric exposure. Second, anchoring propagates selectively: implied P/E ratios shift in the anchor direction, buy/sell recommendations exhibit a sign reversal attributable to dual-channel contamination, and implied growth forecasts remain largely insulated. Third, model susceptibility differs materially: GPT-5mini exhibits substantially weaker anchoring than Claude Haiku and Gemini across all tested conditions. These results imply that model choice and prompt framing are first-order determinants of anchoring risk in LLM-assisted finance tasks and should be empirically validated in practice.

detail.title: Systematic Reversal and Industry Momentum
detail.abstract: Individual stocks exhibit strong one-month reversal, yet industry, characteristic, and factor portfolios display short-term momentum. Contrary to the view that diversification eliminates reversal, we show that a pervasive residual-to-systematic reversal effect---capturing a negative relation between past idiosyncratic returns and future systematic returns---persists even in diversified portfolios. This reversal component depresses observed industry momentum and obscures its economic source. Hedging the reversal substantially improves industry momentum profits and reveals that industry momentum is economically distinct from factor momentum. Standard spanning regressions misattribute the source of industry momentum by omitting this reversal component, whereas Fama-MacBeth regressions are less sensitive to this omission.

detail.abstract: This study employs two discrete choice experiments (DCEs) conducted with two sample groups in Indonesia to investigate the informal settlement upgrading priorities of residents (sample 1) and explore how they align with public taxpayers’ preferences (sample 2). The first DCE explores the relative importance placed upon common planning and public health priorities, such as water security, drainage, and diarrhoea in children, alongside local economic development priorities. The second DCE investigates the relative importance placed upon project implementation design considerations, including project completion time and community consultation. Our findings reveal that residents particularly prioritise improvements in water quality and economic development. While informal settlement upgrading interventions often prioritise improving water, sanitation and hygiene (WaSH) to reduce diarrhoea and other water-borne disease, our study highlights that residents also highly value economic empowerment, underscoring the need for integrated upgrading approaches that address both health and livelihood concerns. Taxpayer perspectives were well-aligned on upgrading outcome priorities, but diverged slightly on project implementation. Whereas residents prioritized minimizing project duration and were less concerned with significant community consultation, taxpayers emphasized generating employment opportunities for residents within project designs. Both groups expressed an aversion to residents bearing full responsibility for resourcing ongoing operations and maintenance, preferring government or shared responsibility, highlighting the need for sustainable funding models. The study highlights the value of DCEs as a tool to support locally-led development, informing upgrading strategies that are more likely to be both politically feasible and successfully appropriated into urban livelihood practices of residents.

detail.title: CDX Markets, Time-Varying Fear, and Corporate Leverage
detail.abstract: CDX spreads and corporate leverage comove strongly and more intensely during crises. Existing CDX pricing models cannot reproduce this pattern because they treat default and capital structure as exogenous. We develop a consumption-based model where firms optimally choose default and leverage while an Epstein-Zin representative agent learns about rare disaster risk. Rising disaster beliefs increase default boundaries and raise leverage, generating a fear-driven financing channel that elevates CDX spreads. We estimate the model to match the 5-year CDX rate, equity returns, and leverage. The model replicates the CDX term structure and physical default probabilities out of sample.

detail.abstract: Reliable knowledge of domestic hot water (DHW) and space heating (SH) energy use in buildings is essential for dimensioning heating systems, evaluating building performance, and modelling energy demand and flexibility. However, while buildings often have main meters for total heat or electricity use, they rarely include submetering that distinguishes between SH and DHW. This paper presents a comparative assessment of five methods from the literature for disaggregating DHW and SH energy use and generating representative DHW load profiles in Norwegian apartment buildings using only aggregated heating data. Four of the methods are rulebased or unsupervised, while the fifth is a supervised CatBoost model trained on random subsets of buildings and applied to others. The methods are evaluated against measured DHW demand in 19 apartment buildings using statistical metrics (R², NMAE, NMBE, CV(RMSE)) and visual inspection of disaggregated loads and daily profiles. Results show that the supervised method performs well when trained and tested on similar buildings but performs poorly when applied to buildings with different characteristics. Among the unsupervised approaches, a method which uses the Building-Profet model to separate temperature-dependent (SH) and temperatureindependent (DHW) components while correcting for seasonal variations, shows the most robust performance across all buildings. The study also finds that standard DHW load profiles commonly used in energy modelling, or methods relying solely on warm-season measurements, provide poor representations of actual DHW energy use in apartment buildings. The paper also recommends accounting for seasonality when developing and applying DHW load profiles.

title: Brief of Amici Curiae Jacob Noti-Victor and Saurabh Vishnubhakat in Support of Appellee and Affirmance, SoundExchange, Inc. v. Sirius XM Radio, Inc., No. 25–2150-cv (2d Cir., Feb. 27, 2026)

detail.title: Brief of Amici Curiae Jacob Noti-Victor and Saurabh Vishnubhakat in Support of Appellee and Affirmance, SoundExchange, Inc. v. Sirius XM Radio, Inc., No. 25–2150-cv (2d Cir., Feb. 27, 2026)
detail.abstract:
Amici support Sirius XM Radio’s position that § 114 of the Copyright Act does not grant SoundExchange a right to sue in federal court to enforce royalty payments under the statute’s compulsory license. Because the statute contains no express authorization for such suits, SoundExchange’s theory depends on the recognition of an implied private right of action. Courts are appropriately reluctant to infer such remedies where Congress has not clearly provided them, given the separation-of-powers concerns that arise when the judiciary supplies a damages remedy not enacted by the legislature. Those concerns carry particular force in the context of § 114. Since establishing the digital public performance right and its accompanying compulsory license in 1995, Congress has repeatedly revisited and refined this statutory regime through a series of targeted amendments. In doing so, Congress has carefully balanced the competing interests of a wide range of stakeholders, including artists, record labels, music publishers, digital and satellite radio services, broadcasters, and the listening public. This sustained legislative engagement reflects deliberate policymaking in a technologically complex and economically significant field. Judicial creation of a cause of action for SoundExchange would intrude upon that policymaking role and risk disrupting the equilibrium Congress has repeatedly negotiated. If SoundExchange seeks expanded enforcement authority, the appropriate avenue is legislative revision rather than judicial implication. Accordingly, the Court should affirm the judgment of the district court.

We gratefully acknowledge our counsel, Russell Rennie of Susman Godfrey LLP.  The arguments expressed in this brief are ours and should not be imputed to Mr. Rennie or his firm.

title: Optimal stopping of ICU treatments under hypothetical interventions - A Scoping Review

detail.title: Optimal stopping of ICU treatments under hypothetical interventions - A Scoping Review

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Giovanni Cinà reports financial support was provided by Kansen voor West.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the Kansen voor West III [project number KVW3-00024].

detail.abstract:
Background: Dynamic treatment regimes (DTR) are a sequence of treatment rules prescribing patient management based on evolving patient characteristics and are typical in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU). Determining the optimal time to stop a specific treatment under a DTR is clinically and computationally challenging: premature stopping can adversely affect patient outcomes, while prolonging it beyond clinical necessity can be harmful, expensive, and resource-intensive. This problem can be mathematically formulated as an Optimal Stopping Problem (OSP), where the goal is to identify the optimal time to stop the treatment that maximizes expected benefit or minimizes harm. OSPs are frequently encountered in treatment decisions, and unbiased decision-making requires causal reasoning to (i) correct treatment-related biases that naive prediction models fail to address, and (ii) enable sequential prediction under hypothetical interventions across all clinically permissible stopping options.  

Aims: In this scoping review, we aimed to identify literature that employ causal methods and facilitate sequential predictions under hypothetical interventions to solve OSPs, with emphasis on ICU applications. We further evaluated how different methodological frameworks address assumptions, estimands, and analytical challenges within the ICU context, emphasizing how experimental settings shape their applicability.  

Methods: Causal reasoning for OSP under DTRs remains understudied in intensive care. To address this gap, we extended the literature search scope to include (i) causal methods under DTRs for OSPs in general healthcare, and (ii) causal methods under DTRs applied to any ICU task. We applied the two search strategies to systematically query PubMed, arXiv, Web of Science, and Scopus from inception to November 3, 2025, screening results according to PRISMA guidelines for scoping reviews. Both methodological and applied studies were included. Additionally, we proposed a set of desiderata to evaluate the applicability of identified approaches to ICU decision-making and their capacity to address OSP. 

Results: We identified 52 relevant studies: 33 from general healthcare, and 19 from ICU settings. The studies originated primarily from epidemiology, biostatistics, and computer science. Each study was systematically evaluated and scored using the proposed desiderata to assess their relevance to ICU decision-making and applicability to OSP. 

Conclusion: Two promising approaches to estimate optimally timed DTRs emerged: (i) target trial emulation with three design patterns - thresholding covariates, sequential trials, and adaptive treatment-length strategies, (ii) algorithmic search with reinforcement learning and sequential decision tree methods. A key contribution of this review is the introduction of desiderata as a structured basis for evaluating methodological suitability to ICU decision-making. More broadly, this work underscores the significance of causal reasoning for the unbiased optimization of sequential treatment durations in intensive care.

title: Rethinking Urban Liveability: A Growth-Adjusted Framework for Assessing City Performance
affiliations: The OJSC "International Bank of Azerbaijan" and

detail.title: Rethinking Urban Liveability: A Growth-Adjusted Framework for Assessing City Performance
detail.abstract: The Economist Intelligence Unit's Global Liveability Index has become the gold standard for assessing urban quality of life, influencing expatriate compensation packages, investment decisions, and urban policy worldwide. However, this paper identifies a fundamental methodological bias: the index inadvertently favors cities with demographic stagnation over those managing dynamic population growth. By examining the 2025 rankings alongside population growth data, we demonstrate that the most 'liveable' cities-Copenhagen, Vienna, and Zurich-grow at rates below 1% annually, while rapidly expanding cities like Lagos, Dhaka, and Delhi, which attract millions of migrants seeking economic opportunity, consistently rank at the bottom. This paper proposes a growth-adjusted framework that categorizes cities into three distinct groups based on annual population growth rates: Low Growth (<1.0%), Moderate Growth (1.0-3.0%), and High Growth (>3.0%). We argue that maintaining a liveability score of 90/100 while absorbing 3% annual population growth represents greater planning capacity and urban resilience than achieving 98/100 with negative growth. The paper concludes by recommending either separate rankings for each category or growth-adjustment factors that credit cities for maintaining quality amid expansion, thereby creating a more nuanced understanding of sustainable urban success.

title: Does spatial inequality matter? Public service accessibility and residents’ happiness in Chinese megacities
affiliations: Hangzhou City University, Hangzhou City University, Zhejiang University of Science and Technology, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Zhejiang University

detail.title: Does spatial inequality matter? Public service accessibility and residents’ happiness in Chinese megacities
detail.abstract: The spatial configuration of public service facilities has been recognized as a critical non-economic factor for subjective well-being, especially in complex and uneven megacities. Existing studies focus mainly on the spatial patterns of single or limited types of facilities, and rarely explore how spatial inequality in public service provision shapes residents’ happiness. To fill this gap, this study examines 10 Chinese megacities by integrating multi-source spatial data with micro-level household survey data to investigate the spatiotemporal evolution of accessibility and spatial inequality across six categories of public service facilities in 2013 and 2021, along with their effects on life satisfaction and job satisfaction. The results found: (1) public service accessibility exhibits “core-periphery” patterns in megacities, with elderly care, cultural, and park facilities showing the steepest decay coefficients at 2.805, 2.112, and 2.155, respectively; (2) accessibility inequality is highest in rural areas (Gini: 0.70-0.90) and lowest in urban areas (Gini: 0.50-0.70); (3) spatial inequality declined by 2.5%-17.1% from 2013 to 2021, with intra-regional differences still dominant but their contribution shrinking from 58%-64% to 48%-53%; (4) life satisfaction and job satisfaction increased by 6% and 8%, respectively, but exhibiting spatial convergence along the urban-rural gradient; and (5) spatial inequality does not significantly impact residents’ happiness, whereas economic security and mental health have greater influence. These findings suggest that in megacities with extensive public service provision, residents’ happiness is shaped more by multidimensional trade-offs in living conditions than by spatial inequality, thereby offering important policy insights for urban sustainable management.

title: Local Officials’ Carbon Pressure and Corporate Financing

detail.title: Local Officials’ Carbon Pressure and Corporate Financing
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether carbon-reduction pressure faced by local government officials affects firms’ access to external finance. Using textual analysis of six authoritative national newspapers, we construct a prefecture-level measure of carbon-reduction pressure. We find that heightened carbon-reduction pressure significantly reduces firms’ access to bank loans, while equity and bond financing remain unaffected. A one-standard-deviation increase in pressure is associated with a 9.7% decline in bank loan inflows. Using officials’ departures from office as an instrumental variable, we establish a causal link between reduced political pressure and expanded bank lending. Mechanism evidence shows that banks respond to carbon-reduction pressure by amplifying political language in annual reports, consistent with heightened political responsiveness. Firms with carbon-reduction innovation capabilities are largely insulated from these credit constraints.

title: Are Impact Investments where they should be?
affiliations: Florida Atlantic University and Florida Atlantic University - Florida Atlantic University, College of Business, Students

detail.title: Are Impact Investments where they should be?
detail.abstract: We examine whether impact investments reach communities with low social mobility using a novel measure of economic connectedness (EC). We then analyze how EC and co-investor composition shape deal characteristics and exit outcomes. We find that impact funds systematically target communities with low EC, a result that remains robust to matching and instrumental variable analyses. At the same time, both the level of EC and co-investment with traditional investors are strongly associated with differences in deal size and monitoring intensity. While impact investors reach the most disadvantaged areas with low EC, exit success is significantly higher for deals co-invested with traditional funds and located in high-EC communities, highlighting a trade-off between impact-oriented allocation and financial performance.

title: Relative Valuation in Precious Metals Markets

detail.title: Relative Valuation in Precious Metals Markets
detail.abstract: Price ratios convey information about the relative valuation of traded assets. We formalize three channels through which changes in the gold-silver ratio affect asset price volatility and test them using intraday futures data for gold and silver from 2009 to 2025. First, valuation pressure, which captures the degree of misalignment between gold and silver, has both short- and long-run effects on future volatility in both markets. Second, re-balancing pressure, reflecting valuation-induced portfolio adjustments, reduces subsequent volatility. Third, attention pressure, linking relative valuation changes to heightened investor attention, leads to modest volatility increases. These effects are stronger for silver, are driven in the short term primarily by gold appreciating relative to silver, and are most pronounced when gold is relatively expensive. Incorporating valuation pressure extracted from the gold-silver ratio improves out-of-sample volatility forecasts. The gold-silver ratio thus captures pricing dynamics relevant for risk management and portfolio allocation.

title: AI Technology Diffusion in the Stock Market
affiliations: Central South University, Shanghai Institute for Mathematics and Interdisciplinary Sciences, University of Padua - Department of Statistical Sciences and Complutense University of Madrid

detail.title: AI Technology Diffusion in the Stock Market
detail.abstract: The AI technology diffusion over the past decade remains less understood. In this paper, we address this question by studying the information content of the “AI technology premium”. We construct novel, unified measures of firm-level AI exposures through product and labor channels and analyze the US stock market from 2012 to 2024. We document a significant and highly time-varying AI technology risk premium. The product premium is positive and driven primarily by large firms, with positive shocks observed only after 2018. In contrast, the labor premium is weaker and is primarily driven by small firms. These patterns result from slow realization processes, varying investor attention, and the complex pricing of uncertainties related to AI adoption. Consequently, our results demonstrate that AI technology adoption represents a multifaceted process characterized by evolving investor perceptions and gradual realization of potential benefits, providing crucial insights for understanding market dynamics in the AI era.

title: From Measurement to Prediction: Supervised Topic Modelling and Ex-Ante Forecasting of Behavioral Customer Engagement
affiliations: University of Birmingham

detail.title: From Measurement to Prediction: Supervised Topic Modelling and Ex-Ante Forecasting of Behavioral Customer Engagement
detail.abstract: In the digital era, with the growing importance of social media platforms, this study advances customer engagement (CE) research by moving from ex-post measurement to ex-ante prediction. While recent social media CE literature has proposed sophisticated measures of CE, most indices are based on public metrics, leaving most of the work descriptive and retrospective in nature. However, marketing practitioners require predictive capabilities to optimise content and timing decisions before posting social media content. Responding to that challenge, this paper extends the CE measurement approach into a predictive modelling framework. The innovation lies in utilising supervised topic modelling (STM), specifically Anchored CorEx, to generate probabilistic indicators of content levers that are systematically integrated into predictive pipelines. The probabilistic lever features (Entertainment, Trendiness), combined with time and brand metadata, are incorporated into five predictive families: Random Forest, XGBoost, Keras MLP, OLS, and KNN. Results on an authentic luxury brand Twitter dataset (2017-2022) show that the proposed model yields satisfying predictive performance, improving both accuracy and rank validity. Notably, the predictive results prove the validity of the entropy-computed behavioral CE approach in extracting valuable information from social media contexts, leveraging ex-ante marketing strategic decision-making for practitioners.

title: AI-Mediated Epistemic Practice in Comparative Education Policy Research

detail.title: AI-Mediated Epistemic Practice in Comparative Education Policy Research
detail.abstract:
The rapid integration of generative AI into academic research has altered not only how policy texts are analysed, but the epistemic conditions under which knowledge about AI governance is produced. This paper offers a methodological–epistemic analysis of AI-mediated knowledge production in comparative education policy research, grounded in a reflexive examination of two parallel studies of international generative AI-in-education guidelines. Both studies draw on the same empirical corpus but mobilise different analytical frames and address different scholarly communities.

Rather than treating generative AI as a neutral research tool or as an autonomous epistemic agent, the paper conceptualises it as a mediating infrastructure that reorganises analytic labour, interpretive risk, and scholarly responsibility. The analysis shows how GenAI collapses front-end tasks such as summarisation and categorisation, producing frame abundance and shifting methodological work toward the selection, justification, and governance of analytical lenses. It also demonstrates how AI-assisted comparison amplifies the risk of false commensurability in cross-cultural policy analysis, intensifying the need for explicit contextualisation.

Synthesising insights across the two cases, the paper advances the concept of AI-mediated epistemic practice to capture how human judgment, analytical framing, cultural–political context, institutional constraints, and AI systems co-shape what counts as valid knowledge. It argues that under GenAI conditions, rigor depends less on descriptive extraction and more on the traceability of interpretive decisions and boundary articulation. The paper concludes by outlining implications for transparency, responsibility, and methodological discipline in AI-supported policy research, particularly in multilingual and multi-cultural settings.

detail.abstract: For the past three decades, enterprise software has been designed to cater to specific activities within organizations. These solutions are tailored to accounting services, treasury management, control management, supply management, commercial matters, and even business forecasting, among other specialties. However, while platforms like SAP and Oracle aim to integrate these functions and create a more global approach, the question remains: is this truly optimal for companies? Our article argues that this specialized approach is inherently flawed. While individual departments may optimize their specific functions, this does not necessarily lead to optimal performance for the company as a whole. Moreover, this approach can be costly and yield subpar results. In the first part of our article, we will explore various problems and case studies that illustrate why this specialized approach is inefficient and often ineffective. In the second and third part, we will demonstrate how advancements in computer science, particularly through the use of Options models and AI-coordinated Option Matrices, can now analyze and rank the decisions of different specialties within an integrated synergy model. This holistic approach enhances overall company performance and budget allocation, achieving the best Return on Equity (ROE) and future revenue strategies. Additionally, we will discuss how effective AI implementation can enable companies to integrate diverse software systems, achieving efficient outcomes without the drawbacks of specialized software. This integration not only improves interdepartmental communication but also serves as a significant step towards creating a Self-Managed Company, even in the absence of native software solutions.

detail.abstract: This book argues that modern societies are entering a new governance regime in which measurement does not merely observe social life but increasingly decides it. Across finance, employment, health, education, platforms, and security, institutions now rely on durable, searchable, and actionable records to allocate access and risk. As these records become interoperable across domains, they compress the plurality of human identity into portable classifications that can trigger binding outcomes. The central claim is that this shift is not only a privacy problem; it is a civilizational problem: the erosion of ambiguity reduces adaptive capacity, hardens social trajectories, and suppresses the experimentation through which societies evolve. To name the mechanism that turns lived reality into administrative truth, the book introduces transcaption (transcription + capture): the industrial process by which complex events are converted into compliance-ready artifacts forms, logs, codes, scores, flags, and standardized categories. Because transcaption is structurally lossy, it strips context, intent, tone, and temporality, enabling low-fidelity representations to outlive their origins as "zombie data." Over time, institutions come to govern the record rather than the person, producing a reversal of epistemic authority in which the database overrides lived experience. The book develops a quantum-sociological framework to formalize these dynamics, including a typology of measurement (from soft, reversible observation to architecturally irreversible recording), an Observational Density Index (ODI) to describe phase-transition pressures, and a Zeno-like account of how continuous measurement inhibits state change encouraging pre-emptive self-collapse through self-censorship, behavioral flattening, and role convergence. It then explains why distinct political economies converge toward the same endpoint via three pathways: stateled design, regulation-led compliance, and market-led drift. A key policy distinction follows: capability (the ability to collect and analyze) is not the same as actuation (the ability to impose civilian consequences). The book argues that collapse becomes civilizational when security-and compliance-derived inferences are allowed to actuate ordinary life as unappealable allow/deny gates. The concluding chapters apply this framework to the monetary transition CBDCs and regulated stablecoins as a non-optional layer of programmable measurement that can complete the shift from observation to control. Finally, the book proposes an ambiguity-preserving design agenda: purpose limitation, non-export of security classifications into civilian scoring, mandatory decay of non-confirmed suspicion, and institutional "firebreaks" that restore contestability, local context, and human-scale discretion preserving the conditions for reinvention and democratic resilience in a digitally legible age.
